speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my attention has been drawn to the editorial in to-day's Globe and Mail entitled "An Unfair Basis." The editorial is the latest move in what appears to be an organized campaign of misrepresentation of the federal government's wartime alcoholic beverage order-

speechtext:
-by representing that the federal government is responsible for the fact that the monthly ration of spirits, authorized in Ontario is thirteen ounces, and in Quebec eighty ounces.
No detailed reply to its allegations is required.
On June 5 I gave to this house a statement showing the exact quantities of liquor allocated to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and showed that there was a difference of only 1-2 per cent between the quantities available in those provinces. It was also shown that the quantity available for Ontario had permitted a ration in that province of 160 ounces a month on the basis of permits outstanding in January, 1943, but that the increase in the number of permits issued by the Ontario Liquor commission from 155,295 in January, 1943, to 1,282,938 in March, 1944, had necessitated a -reduction in the individual ration.
The federal government has nothing whatever to do with deciding what the ration shall be in each province. Each province is entitled to receive 70 per cent of the quantity of spirits released for sale in the year which ended October 31, 1942. In other words, each province receives exactly the same proportion of the quantity consumed in the base period.
While it is true that the per capita quantity of spirits available is very slightly higher in Quebec than in Ontario, the editorial entirely ignores the fact that the per capita quantity of beer available in Ontario is considerably higher than it is in Quebec. The unfair basis, in other worlds, proves to be the editorial itself.
I have also had my attention drawn to a cartoon entitled "Federal Dispensary" which appeared in the same newspaper on June 13, and which suggested the same idea. Under the circumstances, it can only be assumed that the editorial and the cartoon have been published with the deliberate intention of distorting the facts and misleading the public. The Globe and Mail cannot consider that it is assisting the war effort of this country by falsely representing that one province receives preferential treatment over another province, and it can only be assumed that its anxiety to obtain political advantage overrides its interest in our national welfare.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION AND PREVENTION OF FISCAL EVASION

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of -National Revenue):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION AND PREVENTION OF FISCAL EVASION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as was
announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) last week, a tax convention was signed at Ottawa on the 8th of June, 1944. between Canada and the United States of America having for its objects the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion in the case of estate taxes imposed by the United States and the succession duties imposed by the parliament of Canada.
I am now tabling the convention, and in the course of a few days a bill will be introduced for the purpose of ratifying the convention by parliament.
For the information of the house I will give a brief outline of the convention.
Both countries have in the past applied the principle of the deceased's domicile as well as the principle of the local situation of the assets of deceased persons in the taxation of estates. The result has been that in many cases the personal property of deceased owners has been subject to dual taxation-once by the country in which the deceased was domiciled at the time of his death and again by the country in which some or all of his assets were situated at that time.
Real property was the only type of asset which escaped this dual imposition, as both the United States and Canada make no attempt to tax realty situated outside the boundaries of the taxing jurisdiction.
The problem of double taxation was intensified by the fact that the rules applied by the United States of America in determining the local situation of shares and stocks of corporations differ from those applied in Canada. In the United Slates the principle applied was that this class of property was subject to taxation if it was in any way regarded as being under the control of the taxing authority. tMr. Graydon.l
For example, the shares of companies incorporated under the laws of the United States or any of the states and owned by a non-domiciled decedent and physically situated outside the United States at the time of death were deemed to have a situs within the United States regardless of whether the certificate was in the name of the deceased, or in street name, or other bearer form.
In Canada, on the other hand, stocks and shares were regarded as being situated where they coil'd be effectively dealt with, namely, at the place of registration of the securities. Although this principle was much less sweeping in its operation than that in force in the United States, it nevertheless gave rise to considerable trouble in relation to companies having duplicate or multiple share registers.
Some cause of complaint has arisen in the past as to the method of determining the rates of taxation applicable to estates of non-domiciled decedents by reference to the entire value of such estates. Representations have been made that each country should fix the rates of taxation in such cases by the value of the property situated in the country which imposes the tax.
While Canada grants exemptions from taxation in estates of non-domiciled decedents in the proportion that the value of the property in Canada bears to the total value of the deceased's estate, this method of exemption has not been applied so far in the United States. That country grants only a nominal exemption of $2,000 in all cases of non-domiciled decedents, notwithstanding that an exemption of S100,000 is granted in the case of domiciled estates.
With a view to removing these causes of complaint, and particularly in order to avoid double taxation of estates in future, conversations recently took place between the taxing officials of both countries with the result that the tax convention was finally agreed upon.
The main features of the convention may thus be summarized:
Real property is to be taxed exclusively by the country wherein it is situated.
The country of domicile to have the right, at the outset, to tax all the personal property of the deceased, as heretofore.
The country of situs to have the right to tax the property situated within its boundaries.
The taxes paid in the country of situs are to be allowed as a credit against the taxes payable in the country of domicile which includes the same assets for tax purposes. The credit, however, is to be limited to that portion of the tax in the country of domicile that the value of the taxable property abroad

Canadian Forces
is of the total value of the deceased's estate.
There is to be a uniform rule in determining the situs of shares of corporations. These shares are to be deemed to be situated and taxable in the country where the corporation is organized.
While the rules as to situs of other properties vary somewhat in the two countries, it is agreed that for the purpose of the convention, the situs of such other properties is to be determined by the laws of the country imposing the tax.
Each country is to take into account only the property therein situated when taxing the property of persons dying domiciled in the other country.
Exemptions to be granted estates of non-domiciled decedents are to be the same as those granted to estates of domiciled decedents, reduced, however, in direct proportion that the value of the property taxed abroad bears to the total value of the property wherever situated. Canada will benefit considerably by this provision, as, at the present time, the United States only allows an exemption of $2,000 in the case of persons dying domiciled here, but this benefit is now only reciprocal to the benefit Canada always granted to the United States.
Articles VII to XIII of the convention are designed with a view to the exchange of information to prevent fiscal evasion. They are quite similar in scope to the provisions already in force with respect to income tax. By article XIV the convention is given a retroactive operation to 14th June, 1941, being the date when the original Dominion Succession Duty Act came into force. The convention is to remain in force for a period of five years from that date, and indefinitely thereafter, but may be terminated upon six months' notice at the end of the five year period or at any time thereafter.

The hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Dupuis) was kind enough to advise me of his intention to ask this question, and perhaps it is desirable that the confusion which

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
has existed should be cleared up in the public mind. It doubtless arose from the remarks already quoted which the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie made on the third reading of the bill. There was apparently in his mind some confusion based on the difference between those who were called up under the mobilization act and those who were in the reserve army.
As the matter is somewhat technical I believe this house will agree that, in fairness to members, and for the advantage of those in the country who will be affected at the next election, it should be definitely cleared up.
Perhaps I should give a definition of the two forces, not that practically every member does not know it, but apparently the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie was labouring under a certain amount of confusion.
Reserve personnel of the Canadian militia, who are generally described as reserve army personnel, are members of the Canadian army who have not been placed on active service or who are not deemed to be on active service. They are not in full time military employment but are only required to perform a certain number of days training per annum, part of which is carried out in summer camps and the remainder throughout the year in their own localities.
On the other hand a National Resources Mobilization Act soldier is a soldier who has been enrolled and is undergoing training or performing service or duty under the National Resources Mobilization Act or the regulations passed pursuant thereto. Upon his being enrolled in the army a National Resources Mobilization Act soldier is deemed to be and is placed on active service pursuant to the Militia Act. In this respect and because he is in full time military employment his position is entirely different from that of a member of the reserve army as mentioned above.
Bearing in mind those definitions, provision is made that everyone called up under the mobilization regulations who is performing training, service or duty in any of the naval, military or air forces, regardless of age, may vote as a war service elector wherever he may be stationed and whether it be within Canada or elsewhere.	*
On the other hand, one serving in the reserve army may also vote as a war service elector but requires to be of the full age of twenty-one years, absent from his ordinary place of residence while undergoing training at a duly authorized training camp or school established for full-time courses, or has been called up on service by the Minister of National Defence. This includes a member
of the university air training corps or a member of the air cadet corps who is at present in the course of duty at a Royal Canadian Air Force unit.
This will, I trust, remove the confusion which might otherwise be created by the remarks of the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, June 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of bill No. 83, to establish a department of veterans' affairs.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
During the past few days a great many members of the house have engaged in debate on the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie Kingl to give second reading to bill No. 83, an act to establish a department of veterans-^ affairs. I think we can agree that practically every aspect of rehabilitation, especially as it. applies to the ex-servicemen, has been touched upon by the members. I realize therefore that in speaking upon the measure at this time one is likely to engage in a certain amount of repetition. I shall endeavour as far as possible to avoid that fault. It is quite obvious I think that the members of the house generally speaking are agreed upon the desirability of establishing a separate department for the express purpose of handling those measures-relating to our ex-servicemen. I believe I am. quite correct in saying also that that feeling is shared by the people of Canada and would also be supported by the service personnel. I would hasten to add however that the mere establishment of a department of this nature does not of necessity guarantee that our ex-servicemen will be given that complete consideration which some of us believe they deserve. If this were a department for any other purpose I might have a tendency to oppose it. I say that for the reason that generally speaking the tendency of government, to expand, grow and take in new territory, increase its payroll and so forth, is something that must be guarded against; but I propose, to deal with that on another occasion.
Between 1914 and 1918 the constituency which I have the honour to represent gave very generously of its men to the armed forces. Following the cessation of hostilities at that.
3SS0

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
time many of our men returned to that constituency, but unfortunately there were men who did not. Of those who did return a few things might well be said at this -time. First, we have those who were partly, and in some cases, almost totally disabled. We realize that because of the involved regulations and restrictions many of those who did return in that physical state found themselves without pensions. Just how general that may have -been I do not propose to hazard a guess, but suffice it to say that a great many of them did return in a disabled condition, and because of some harsh restriction or because of some technicality they were deprived of their just due.
Then again we had a number of those who were disabled who were fortunate enough to secure a pension. History records that in all too many cases those pensions were hopelessly inadequate. The result was that many of those partly disabled veterans endeavoured to find employment in the labour market in competition with those who were physically fit. Then there were many of our ex-servicemen who were established under the Soldier Settlement Act. My colleague, the hon. mem-bero for Battle River (Mr. Fair) did not leave anything unsaid in dealing with those soldier settlers. I wish to say that I concur in what he said. I heartily endorse his remarks and subscribe fully to his claim that these settlers should be granted clear title to their homes.
If I may just go back to the commencement of the operation of that scheme, in my -constituency we found, as was found everywhere in Canada, these veterans were placed upon land which was valued at, I dare say, twice its -present-day value. Machinery and stock was provided at inflated prices and, as was stated by the hon. member for Battle River, the interest charge of five per cent on the debt was out of line, as was the seven percent charged on the arrears. It is not necessary for me to trace the history of that settlement programme during the subsequent years. We know that of the total only a few were successful in acquiring clear title to their property. Many of them paid more than the property -was ever worth in the first place, and yet were in the position of still owing more than the price at which the land should have been sold to them in the beginning.
As one travels about in his constituency or elsewhere and has occasion to visit with and talk to these veteran settlers of the first world war, ones heart is torn because in many' instances they are men of fifty-five, sixty-five, and, yes, seventy years of age. They have tried; they have worked hard, and while it is true you may find the very few who could have done better, that cannot be sa-id of the
{Mr. Shaw.]
majority. They did their -best, and, as I said a moment ago, paid more than the land was worth. And yet they are faced with this situation: -periodically they are threatened with cancellation of the confract and offered a lease agreement made for a period of one year. In other instances they have been given new contracts for a period of twenty-years. I am bound to say' that it is fantastic to offer a man sixty-five years of age a twenty-year contract and imply that at the end of twenty years he will have paid for the property and will become the owner of it.
I wish to repeat that there is a general feeling in -my part of the country at least that unless we are prepared to do justice to those veterans of the first world war there is little hope for the right thing being done for the veterans of this war. Some may say that that feeling is not justified, but it exists, and in a measure I feel the same way. I do not like to deal with individual cases of pensions, and I shall not do it by name, but I have encountered a large number of cases where a man was expected to subsist on a pension of $4 or $5 a month. I recall one case in particular, that of a man who attained the rank of sergeant-major. During the last war he spent almost four years in France. He suffered a concussion and was gassed, and as a result was sent to hospital. After a number of months in hospital he was returned to Canada and discharged. For a period of seventeen years he was obliged to try to get by on $3.75 a month. It is true that he was able to work part-time, but he probably worked for three or four days and then was sick for a couple of weeks. I would not -mention that case if it were the only one of which I have information. It happens so frequently that I hope no one will ever be able to say that out of this war will come veterans who are obliged to try to get by on pensions of that type.
I have also -had brought to my attention a number of cases in which, upon discharge, the soldier was refused pension outright, regardless of the fact that he produced all the affidavits and other documents necessary to prove -that there had been a very serious deterioration in the state of his health as a result of -his service. He was refused repeatedly; then, probably nine or ten- years after the cessation of hostilities, he was finally conceded a small pension. One case still stands out in my memory. The veteran himself is now dead; it is a wonder he lived as long as he did, considering the treatment he received. This man was discharged in 1919, but n-ot until 1927 did they finally agree that he was deserving of a pension, or, in other words that his disability -was attributable to

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
war service. It seems to me a remarkable thing that it should take any commission nearly ten years to determine that fact. This man died in 1939, after which his widow received nothing. The pension was very small, only $15, but with the loss of it the widow was obliged to go out into the labour market and endeavour to obtain employment in order that she might live. I have a number of cases of the kind, and I sincerely .trust that as a result of these experiences we may learn and, more important, that we may make good use of that knowledge.
Again in this war my constituency has given generously of its men and women. Many of them are the sons and daughters of veterans of world war No. 1. In instances to which I could refer specifically I have fought the cases of their parents; yet, regardless of the unfortunate deals which their parents received, these young people were prepared to and did answer the call of their country for help. In one or two cases it was surprising to me that this should be so, bearing in mind the unfortunate experience of their parents. Men from my constituency have served in every theatre of war in which the Canadian forces have served. We have had our causalties, unfortunately, but so have the other parts of Canada. We have had men killed; we have had men permanently disabled. Some men whom I know personally are in German prison camps, and I am very proud to be able to say that a number of our men, from my home town and elsewhere, were with the third division when it stormed the coast of France. I know those boys are standing up to .their responsibilities in magnificent fashion. I was quite impressed by the remarks of one hon. member who spoke yesterday, I believe one of the Winnipeg members, who said in effect that no material consideration can repay these heroes of ours for the sacrifices they are making to ensure the freedom and security of this nation. I hold the view quite firmly, Mr. Speaker, that, money cannot make up for the loss of life. I do not believe that anything we can give a man can make up for the loss of a limb or any other serious physical disability. Much less can w'e make up with money for t-he ravages of spiritual and mental anxiety, which may be the highest price he has to pay.
During the months and years which have gone by I have had a good deal of correspondence with men in the services. I read their letters with the utmost care, for one reason because I want to ascertain what they [DOT]may be thinking with respect to their postwar possibilities and opportunities. Sometimes it is said that these boys who are engaged in battle are not concerned about the future,
that they know they have a job to do and that they believe the future will take care of them. I do not entirely subscribe to that view, from the correspondence I have received.
I am going to repeat one or two sentences from a letter I received from one of our young men in an overseas theatre of war. These may not be his exact words, but they are as close as I get them, not having his letter immediately at hand. He said:
We are supposed to ;be fighting to safeguard the democratic ideals and to preserve the sovereign integrity of our nation. When uar ends and I return-
I recall so well that he had in brackets "if I do return"-
-shall I be given the opportunity to share in the wealth which I fought to save? Shall I be given an opportunity to own part of the land which I fought to save?
I want to emphasize that he seemed to lay stress on the word "opportunity." He was not asking that everything be handed to him when he returned; all he asked was an opportunity. In my reply to that boy among other things I said:
In my opinion the least Canada can offer is a chance to share in the wealth and in the heritage of culture and scientific progress which you and your comrades are saving from the clutches of aggressor nations.
Probably I should have added, "not only to share, but to share on a fair and equitable basis with all others." These boys in the service who are doing a job, and doing it well, are quite properly looking to us at home to see to it that when they return it will be to a country worthy of their magnificent courage, of their sacrifices and of the ideals for which they are fighting. In my opinion this obligation constitutes an essential responsibility confronting every last Canadian. I know that there is a tendency on the part of some to look to a government or to a particular group of people to bring about the very desirable results to which I have referred, but I really feel that this great problem of taking care of our service men and women when the war is over is the responsibility of all Canadians in all parts of Canada.
In 1939 Canada entered this war with a great deal of determination. At that time total employment in Canada amounted to about 4,000,000-1 am speaking only roughly. Within a period of four years we had increased our employment to approximately 5,000,000. Out of that number approximately 2,000,000 were in the armed services, or were engaged in providing the machines of war, or were producing those things necessary for war export purposes.
The point I wish to emphasize in that regard is this: We did enter the war with great

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
zeal and determination, and we accomplished things which only a month or so before the outbreak of war were regarded as being utterly and completely impossible. We also took our men from the streets-and from the mines, the farms and the factories. We pointed out to them their duty, and. they responded cheerfully and magnificently. We took that boy from the street, the boy who had never been able to find employment, the boy who could not secure a decent wage while he was on the street-if, indeed, any wage at all-and we provided for him not only his clothing, but dental, medical, optical, hospital, educational and other services. We armed him and paid him. We also transported him to the theatre of war. Those boys are well aware to-day that, because of our determination to utilize-and I shall use an oft-used term- the wealth and the production of the country, we were able to attain that degree of achievement which was most desirable.
In some parts of Canada we hear it said, and we read it in publications, that it was only because of the great need and because of such unusual determination that we were able to accomplish the things it was necessary to accomplish in war-time, but that after the war we cannot hope to be able to accomplish so much in the field of non-war activities. I do not subscribe to that view at all. I say that when the war is over and when our lads return we shall have a country poorer only in the sense that we have lost so many of our youth. But we shall have a country developed as it has never been developed before, with a productive capacity not dreamed *of in days gone by. All we must do is accept it as our responsibility, so that when these lads come back we shall be able to say, "We have that which is necessary to give you what you have earned because of your contribution." During the course of the debate several members have pointed out, in definite terms, the things we must guarantee to our boys upon their return.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your leniency up to the present point. I had really completed what I wanted to say in that regard.

In my opinion when these lads return we should be prepared to guarantee them full pay and allowances of the rank of private until such time as they are able to fit themselves into the economic life of the country. By that I do not mean that our boys returning from overseas should of necessity be retained in uniform. One hon. member indicated a day or two ago that the boys were anxious to get this whole thing over and get out of uniform. In advocating that we guarantee to them full pay and allowances to the rank of private until such time as we absorb them into the economic life of the country, I am not advocating that they be retained in uniform against their will.
I say, too, that to those same men we must guarantee hospitalization and treatment for illness, without the application of the previous policy of deducting pay for such attention from their incomes. Further than that, it is most essential that in respect of the dependents of those killed while in service we should make full and adequate provision for pensions at a figure no less than the full rate of pay of a private, including dependents' allowances. Then, in respect of children more than eighteen years of age, to supplant dependents' allowance there should be an educational grant of a sum sufficient to enable them to secure the education which their parents might have been able to provide had the father been at home.
What I say in that regard must also apply to the men of the merchant marine. To my mind it is a tragedy that those men, who are probably playing just as important a part in the prosecution of the war as are our troops

and I do not say this in any disparaging way at all-find themselves extolled in song and story but almost entirely forgotten when it comes to the securing of benefits received by members of the armed services.
I had brought to my attention not loqg ago the case of a man who had served two years in the merchant marine, and who was discharged only recently because of his physical condition. He had reached the age of sixty years. That man had served in the north Atlantic, the south Atlantic and the Indian ocean, and yet, following his discharge, when I pressed for consideration in connection with having the interest rate on his soldier settlement contract reduced from 5 per cent to 3i per cent, I was told that unless he was pensioned, favourable consideration could not be given to his application. The hard part in the letter I received in reply was the statement by the minister to the effect that after all, the process of reducing his interest rate from 5 per cent to 3i per cent would mean a saving of only $20 a year. I thought that

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
was cold, and perhaps just a little brutal.
In other words, they said that since it was only $20 a year-which might mean a great deal to that man-they should not be too greatly concerned about granting it to him.
0 I should like to say a few words in connection with the present policy for establishing our soldiers on the land. The hon. member for Battle River indicated that he proposed discussing this matter at some length at the appropriate time. Let me say that I agree the present Veterans' Land Act is an improvement over the old Soldier Settlement Act. But this is a thought which repeatedly passes through my mind, and has been brought to my attention on many occasions: Provide the veteran with a parcel of land, provide him with an equity in that property, provide him with a lower rate of interest than he has ever enjoyed before, and yet after you have done all those things, he is still left at the mercy of an internal economic system which may ruin and crush him completely. Even under the Veterans' Land Act the man so established cannot possibly weather the gale if he is subjected to the conditions to which the soldier settlers of the last war were subjected during the early thirties. It would be utterly and completely impossible.
And so I assert that hand in hand with all the schemes for the rehabilitation of our soldiers after the war there must be a complete and full realization that unless we give careful thought and consideration to the making of very necessary changes in the economic structure of this country, we shall find that we have failed in our attempt to bring about the results which I think we are all agreed are so necessary.
I have not endeavoured to go into any details, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the veteran measures which the government have proposed. I do not think it should be necessary that we should press, for instance, for an adequate clothing allowance. The government should know what is an adequate and what is an inadequate clothing allowance, and that principle applies to the whole fipld of reestablishment. Just let the officials put themselves in the position of the individual who is coming back after the war; consider all the benefits and consider all the obstacles; and then ask themselves the fair and square question:	W ould I regard this as being
adequate? I know that if the present inadequate clothing allowance is increased to $125, some may press for $150. I know it is completely impossible to please everyone. But if the government themselves would do that thing which they themselves would be satisfied with if they were in the position of the returning service man, many of the disabilities which crop up under these different types of reestablishment measures would probably never occur.
In conclusion, may I express the hope that after this war we shall not have a repetition of what occurred after the last war, that we shall have nothing not even remotely resembling the conditions which developed after the last war. We owe that to our men. They are looking to us for it, and I think, Mr. Speaker, that we are big enough to do the job. This does not constitute any utopian dream-I hear that phrase used so frequently. When I advocate what I regard as being only limited justice to the veteran, I always hear someone expressing the idea that it is just another utopian dream. In my opinion there is nothing more potent in building up morale among the service men than the knowledge that the ideals for which our boys are fighting to-day are on the way to becoming the realities of to-morrow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is perfectly true that all our thoughts are centred on the invasion front at this time and what is happening there. While it is most desirable that the business of the house be expedited, nevertheless it is only natural that any measure affecting the men ind the women in our armed forces, especially those who are at the moment fighting our battles overseas, will create considerable interest and discussion in the house. While, generally speaking, Mr. Speaker, on the second reading of a bill only the principle may be discussed, one cannot discuss intelligently the many changes that have been made in the measure now before us unless one deals with more than the mere principle of the bill. With the principle I am in hearty accord.
First of all let me say that the grouping together of all the various departments dealing with veterans' affairs under one ministry will I believe meet the wishes and the points of view of all our citizens. Let me here express one personal wish regarding that ministry. It is my hope, and I believe I speak the thought of many members of the house and many people outside, that the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) will be left long to carry out the duties that it will be necessary to perform under the new set-up. I was pleased to see that in the act national health is separated from pensions. The national health of our people has become a most important subject, and we are taking such notice of it that to separate this subject from pensions is to my mind certainly a step in the right direction.
A little later I wish to deal with one aspect of the bill relating to the Veterans' Land Act,

Uepartme.nl of Veterans' Affairs
as I have one or two matters to discuss with regard to its operations.
The other day one of the members-I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair)-suggested when speaking to the house that in the setting up of . a new department and the appointment of new officials every consideration be given to the young men of this war. With that view I think we are all in accord. But as one who has taken a great interest in pension matters may I say that what is more particularly desired is that the officials appointed should have a sympathetic frame of mind rather than one seeking to conform too strictly to the letter of the act. It is not generally known and recognized throughout the country, and many members of parliament still fail to recognize, that even the minister himself will be governed and is governed by the Pension Act. Therefore it seems to me important that the officials who are handling the administration, those behind the scenes having to do with the appeals coming before them, be men of sympathy and understanding. There is not a great deal of complaint in that regard at the present time, but such was not always the case.
I well remember, and so will every member of the house, that during the years from 1930 to 1935 or 1936 there were officials in that department who were not always as sympathetic to the appeals and requests made by returned men as many of us thought they should be. In those days, too, the pension advocates were not always as vigorous as they might have been. It was my impression after presenting many claims on behalf of returned men that some of the pension advocates were a little hesitant in putting forth all the fight within them on behalf of the cases they had in hand. I got that impression after observing their efforts' at some of these hearings. They were perhaps a little afraid that those in authority at Ottawa, not particularly the minister, but the officials in authority, might not wish that too many favourable decisions be given.
Mention was made by one member speaking yesterday of the mefnbers of the treasury board. I have a severe criticism to make regarding the treasury board. After all, it is not the minister who will handle the pension cases. Once the act is in effect, appeals go before the pension commissioners and their officials. They sit as a court, and after their decision is given in a case it is my opinion that their decision, if favourable, should be final. I have personal knowledge of case after case where, after the decision had been given, officials of the treasury board undertook to' look over the case and either reduced the pen-
[Mr. Reid.J
sion or declared that it should not be given. I believe the country is tired of that kind of control.

speechtext: That has not been done recently, has it?

speechtext:
I know of one recent case in which it was done. It is true that there must be some control over expenditures; but surely, after a man's history file has been looked into, after the entire case has been investigated, no official from some other department or branch should sit in judgment upon that man's case and act to his detriment. I ask the minister to endeavour at least to see to it that treasury board officials keep their hands off the cases, especially in which, after the circumstances have been gone into, a favourable decision has been given.
One matter I would ask the minister to take note of in the new set-up relates to the provision whereby pensions can be granted under what is known as the meritorious clause. I was surprised to find how few pensions had been granted under this provision. No pension commissioner with whom I have discussed the matter has been able to define what the meritorious clause really means. I mention this particularly because the present war is entirely different from that of 1914-18, and there will be many men coming back who have flown planes over Germany, and who may have to outward appearance no bodily injury, but who must have suffered; so in the handling of cases under the meritorious clause a new interpretation will have to be given to it in order that those appealing under it may have a chance of obtaining a pension.
Despite what the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Han sell) said the other day, I believe that every member of the House of Commons and the people generally are agreed that no monetary considerations should be placed in the way of providing our returned men with pensions. That principle is generally accepted. Although ho-n. members may not always applaud it in the house, I think it is only fair to say that every one of us is agreed that financial conditions shall not be allowed to obstruct adequate provision for tho.se men who have given so willingly and freely of their lives, and but for whom we of this House of Commons might to-day not be here.
May I also draw the attention of the minister to the desirability of building or procuring smaller hospitals apart from the general hospital which is usually designated as that to which all returned men must go.
I believe that a condition we have m British Columbia is not dissimilar to conditions in other provinces. I know how difficult it is for a man say in the Fraser Valley to reach

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
the Vancouver Shaughnessy hospital; in fact, from so short a distance as forty miles it will take him at least the entire day to go to Shaughnessy hospital and return. I recognize that it is desirable to assemble in one large building all the paraphernalia, the up-to-date equipment and machines required to examine and treat men who are sick. Nevertheless it may be well to give some thought to the setting up of smaller hospitals to which men with minor complaints, requiring perhaps only one or two days' treatment, could resort instead of having to spend a great deal of time in going to and attending at larger institutions. There are indeed cases wherein the time element may mean the difference between life and death.
The desirability of providing work was mentioned the other day as important, and it is important. I suppose every hon. member has had much fhe same experience as I have. From 1930 to 1939 the number of appeals received by members of parliament from men who either wanted a pension or wanted it increased was enormous, but after 1939 the number dropped, proving to me at least that if suitable work could be provided, many of the economic ills from which these men were suffering or thought they were suffering would disappear. So that to my mind at least, the provision of useful work is most important, particularly to our returned men, who should come first.
There are one or two things I want to say with regard to the Veterans' Land Act. I would point out to the house that if those of us from western Canada take up the time of the house on this subject it is because the four western provinces, including British Columbia, had more applications for settlement on the land than did the other provinces. It is interesting to know that of the 25,000 who applied for help to go on the land under the soldier settlement board after the last great war, over 20,000-to be exact, 20,736- were from the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.
As regards the new Veterans' Land Act, it is an improvement upon the old Soldier Settlement Board Act, but I believe that one factor which will militate against the successful carrying out of this measure will be that many of the old sores which arose from the last Soldier Settlement Act still remain. I am not going to take up the time of the house on this occasion in reading personal letters, but when one realizes that only 3,833 claims have not been paid, I do not think it is too much to ask that these be cleaned up and that we have a new deal and a fresh start all round. I was one of those who advocated this
when the Veterans' Land Act was before the house, and I still believe that what I then advocated is the proper policy. I do so after twenty years of experience amongst returned soldiers in British Columbia, and I know that one of the things which put most of them out of business was the load of interest. Of 25,000 men who recently made applications to go on the land, 13,550 did not make good. I use these words advisedly because I do not think it is proper to say that they failed. In the words of the man in the street, the cards were stacked against them before they went on the land.
I do not wish to rehash the past, but it is well known that the government at that time, not having any plan, were not particular where the men went so long as they did not congregate in the cities and were spread out in the rural communities throughout most of the provinces. When I look over the financial statement and realize that over $25 million has been paid in interest, it is to me staggering indeed. The exact amount of interest paid to the present time is $25,381,060. When one realizes that only 3,883 have repaid their loans, which is equal to only fifteen per cent, it means that interest payments made by all who participated in the scheme from the inception of the act to the present time must have averaged between $1,500 and $2,000 each, plus of course cost of administration. Total administration cancellations, as pointed out yesterday by the member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), amounted to $88 million, which also is a staggering amount of money.
I still believe that even at this late date, before placing these men on the land we consider placing them on property that is interest free, because if the man did have a few lean years he would know that his debt would not increase. One can produce case after case where men paid more than their whole principal amount and still owe at least fifty per cent of the original debt. What effect will the condition of these men have on the new settlers going on the land? I say it will have a disastrous effect.
The government of British Columbia have set aside one million acres of land which they are offering to the dominion government on which, if desired, returned men can be settled; but there is one proviso in it which does not make the offer so good, and that is that the men settling on the million acres shall be soldiers who left British Columbia. That means that' soldiers from other provinces will not be allowed to settle on any of the million acres in the interior. I have been in British Columbia from 1909, quite a number of years, and from my experience of that province I would say that not many who were born in

Department of Veterans' Affairs
British Columbia would care to go and live anywhere on that million acres offered by the provincial government; they would prefer to be nearer the larger cities on the coast.
Then there is the cost of clearing. When the new department is set up, the minister, I suggest, might have the whole area surveyed, because first of all there are no men from the outside provinces to be allowed there, and secondly the men who will go there, if any men who do go there, will be very few indeed, and the land has to be cleared. A scheme could be brought about whereby those from the services or others could be utilized to clear the land to make it habitable. But what is more important-and this is the proposition I put to the government-is that instead of centering most of our energies and thoughts on land and farms for the men coming back we should centre our thoughts and activities on the providing, for the men who come back, of modern homes. I think that it will be generally agreed that one of the things first desired by most of us is that we should have a house to live in, and many of the ranches and properties which the men will be asked to go on have not the proper houses. To my mind nothing will make a man more discontent with his lot than to be compelled to live in some old shack.
I would ask the minister to consider providing houses, and I suggest that that should be made the first requirement, instead of concentrating on putting the men on the land. I would point out to the minister, and he knows it as well as I do, that so far as British Columbia is concerned, the fight which the men will have to put up there if they are to do well is going to be harder than in some other provinces, owing to the fact that in that province we have little or no industries.
What has happened since 1939? It is evident that what is required is some financial help if one is to maintain oneself on one of the ranches or farms in the Fraser valley or in British Columbia. Since 1939 hundreds upon hundreds of our citizens have left those places. WThy? First of all, they wanted to help in the war effort, and, second, they needed financial assistance, or wages or salaries on which to live, which they did not have prior to the commencement of the war.
I mention these thoughts because I am a little fearful that the present Veterans' Land Act, good though it may seem to some, will not be all that some people claim it to be or hope it will be. After the experience we have had in British Columbia, and after the heartbreaking scenes I have witnessed, I would urge that the minister, even at this late date, give further consideration to the whole mat-
[Mr. Reid.)
ter, and in the light of some of the thoughts I have expressed this afternoon.
In closing, I want to add one word in praise of the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) for the interest he has taken in, and the work he has done on behalf of, the returned men and for the good of the department as well. I believe that a word of encouragement is due him and I am voicing it on this occasion, feeling sure that many members will agree with the views I have just stated.

speechtext:
I have followed with a great
deal of interest the last two speeches delivered by my colleagues who have resumed their seats, but the anxiety is always the same: What shall we do with the hundreds of .thousands of our young men and women after the war? How will it be possible to re-establish in civil life all these veterans with broken careers and often broken lives in this terrible conflict? No one can answer this tremendous question, not even the government; nevertheless it will be the great task of the authorities to give all possible assistance to the veterans not only of the present but also of the former war.
(Translation):	Notwithstanding the de^
votion and efficiency of the army medical units and nursing services in this war which, through its terrific speed and mobility, is causing the death of thousands and thousands of men, let Canada be prepared for the return of disabled, wounded and crippled soldiers in still greater numbers than in 1918.
While I was alone, with the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix), in opposing to the utmost our participation in this war and the mobilization of our manpower and financial resources, even before those two grievous mistakes had been made, I cannot at this time shrink from the duty of urging the government which declared war to help the veterans of this war and the last conflict.
Let us see the results of a policy that I have repeatedly condemned. Canada will have to assume the task of reestablishing in civilian life an army of one million men and women. They will have to rehabilitate, in entirely new occupations if that is still possible, hundreds of thousands of young men and women. Those of our veterans who had positions in the public service will be fortunate indeed if they are not displaced by newcomers from the British isles and Palestine. That is what happens now. At a time when our sons are shedding their blood in the invasion of the European continent and many are fighting on other

3S87
Department oj Veterans' Affairs
theatres, a large number of people are entering this country under the protection of an unspeakable policy. I should like to know what the government are doing and will do on behalf of our own people?
The Selective Service is already unable to absorb our demobilized soldiers, just as the government was unable after the last war to find for our veterans jobs worthy of their sacrifices.
I have received numerous complaints from veterans of the last war even during this conflict. Such complaints have come to me from all provinces. In many cases, our veterans were established with their families on lands that were unfit for cultivation, while bureaucrats newly-arrived in this country, were taking the best positions in the Canadian civil service. That was greatly to their advantage, of course, but what a shame for us! Let room first be made for our own people. Since the government want to establish a department of veterans' affairs and this bill provides for a considerable increase in the number of government positions, let them reinstate without any formal procedure the mobilized civil servants who, having undergone a few months of training in the armj% are looking for employment because they have been rejected. The oft-stated policy in this regard is not respected. What is the use of establishing a new department if we merely mark time?
As regards national health, I wish to quote an excerpt from page 12 of the publication Canada at War for April, 1944, under the heading "Health Service Survey":
An over-all picture of Canada's existing health services is given in a report of the Canadian Medical Procurement and Assignment Board, tabled in the House of Commons on March 13, 1944. The primary function of the board, which was set up in July, 1942, was to determine the number of medical personnel available to the armed forces and at the same time to try to preserve adequate medical service for civilians. The resulting complete and detailed survey of all branches of medical service together with recommendations for the improvement of existing conditions will enable the government to tackle present problems and plan for the future.
In all branches of medicine civilian demands have increased in inverse ratio to services available. The war has recruited only the healthy and left the physically weaker in disproportionate ^ numbers.	The birth rate has
considerably increased, and the old age population is increasing. (The Dominion Bureau of Statistics estimates that the number of persons GO years of age and over will increase by 20 per cent in the next ten years.) The old and the very young require most medical care. During war-time there is a greater threat of epidemics, especially in the crowded industrial centres. At the same time the increase in national income and economic means has boosted the demand for medical service.
10U-245J
Did the government recognize the invaluable services rendered by civilian physicians to the public and to the army? Quite the contrary, scorning their devotion to duty and their ability, after over-burdening them during the first three years the Mobilization Act was in effect, it cancelled their examination reports and summoned the draftees anew before army physicians and a small number of civilian physicians assigned for that purpose. Not satisfied with having shown itself so ungrateful towards these professional men who gave up both their time and their practice for the benefit of the state, the government now plans to strike the medical profession in Canada a deadly blow by installing state medicine. Let us beware! The day when politics shall interfere with the medical profession, we will witness not only a most disastrous act of injustice but also the decline of national health. When the federal government undertook to legislate on national health, it infringed on provincial prerogatives. It has been doing so for almost thirty years. That sphere does not belong to the Ottawa government. If we read the constitution of the country-

speechtext:
The present debate is concerned with the setting up of a veterans' and national health department. In any case, I have very little more to say. If we read the constitution of the country, provided we do not have to go to London for it, we will find that the bill providing for the establishment of a department of veterans' affairs is unconstitutional as it infringes upon the rights of the provinces.
One word more. Due to the war, misconduct and immorality are permeating our youth. Hence, diseases oft incurable are on the increase and the deadly germs already undermining our present generation will afflict our descendants. It will take more than legislation to prevent such a calamity from spreading to the manpower of a whole nation.
The evil must be warded off by all preventive means at the disposal of medical science and the governments. Otherwise, the disastrous effects of permanent epidemics, pointed out by the highest medical authorities, as reported in the April issue of Canada at War, will be equalled only by the improvidence of our government. I require no other proof than the unfortunate wrecks who live on the State and by the State. Are they to be blamed? No. They are rather to be pitied. Heaven knows what efforts the public authori-

Department of Veterans' Affairs
ties should expend in this field, the most important for the maintenance and the survival of the nation.
In conclusion, I wish to state that centralization is not the remedy to our worst evil. Let the federal authorities be free to cooperate as far as possible with provincial administrations to this end.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the explanatory note in this bill states:
The purpose of this bill is to establish a department of veterans' affairs under the direction of a minister of veterans affairs who shall be responsible for the care, treatment, training, or reestablishment in civil life of ex-members of the armed forces and of persons otherwise engaged in pursuits relating to the war, and for the care of the dependents of such persons.
I do not know who are the " persons otherwise engaged in pursuits relating to the war," but perhaps at some future time the minister can advise us. In the past hon. members of '.this house had a great deal to do with the matter of pensions. My first suggestion to the minister is that when the new department is set up, a proper, comprehensive directory of all the subdepartments and branches be compiled and published, because I believe in that way a great deal of time can be saved. Certainly I am in favour of setting up this new department of government. As I have indicated, all hon. members of this house have had to do with difficult pension cases from time to time, and I believe generally our experience has been that when these cases have been brought to the attention of the proper authorities they have been dealt with satisfactorily. However, I do not think it should be necessary to do that, and I hope that with the setting up of this department that situation will be remedied. I believe a department of this kind should have been set up a long time ago; certainly it would have saved us all a great deal of trouble.
There has been much official propaganda designed to create the impression that Canada leads the world in connection with the rehabilitation and treatment of returned men. No doubt this is so in regard to many aspects [DOT]of the matter, but in my opinion it is not a *question of comparison with any other system in the world. I know all hon. members have tried to offer constructive criticism when veterans' affairs have been under consideration, and have put forward their views in a nonpartisan spirit. But it seems to me that up to the present in connection with veterans' matters everything has been done on the basis of a Teluctant, half-hearted acceptance of proposals advanced by the opposition and supported by public opinion. I cite, for example, the attitude of the government in connection with

Christie street hospital and new military hospitals in general, as well as the matter of the clothing and rehabilitation allowances. There we saw a reluctant acceptance of our proposals. That was also the case in days gone by in connection with the discharge of these men and their pay during hospitalization. There has always been a reluctance to comply with our requests, which I believe has caused the veterans great hardships in the past.
As I have stated, the government seem to have been working on a basis of comparison with other countries instead of making up their mind on a definite policy as to what is right and just for the men returning from overseas. Now, in this preelection session, we see many improvements being put forward by the government. Almost it seeems as though the government have held back the announcement of these improvements until just before an election, to the detriment of the returned men. Well, that did not seem to do much good in connection with the election we heard about only the other day in Saskatchewan, and in view of the results of that election I doubt very much' whether a federal election will be called within the near future. In any case the reluctance of the government in connection with these matters will not be overlooked.
We all know that many mistakes have been made in the past. Following the last war there were mistakes that *were due to lack of experience in the handling of these matters, but many injustices were brought about by an endeavour on the part of various governments to save a little money for the taxpayers. Many examples of the petty paring of pensions and allowances could be mentioned, but the money saved amounted to only a drop in the bucket as compared with the suffering endured by many of our returned men. As an instance I might mention the reluctance of the government to increase the pensions of widows. Each year we have brought up the matter; each year the pensions have been increased slightly. Again, mistakes were made in the past by discharging men from the army too soon, and through the lack of proper papers. No man should be discharged until he has been given a full account of himself by the proper authorities; with his enlistment papers completely filled out, with his physical condition on discharge completely set out, and in short with his full record for the future. Hon. members will recall the difficulties they have had in connection with pensions, arising from the fact that applicants for pensions did not supply sufficient information. Care must be taken to give instructions to the men with regard to their rights, and as to what they

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
should do to have mistakes corrected in their papers at the time of discharge from the army; it should not be left until later. Many heartaches and hardships can thus be avoided.
Regulations are to be set up in connection with this legislation. The regulations should be promulgated and published at the earliest possible moment, because, after all, the bill is comprehensive and covers many features of pensions legislation. Certainly a consolidation should be made of all the regulations, so that in fairness to the returned men, and those who are endeavouring to look after them, justice may be done.
Then, is there any reason why men who have served in the forces, but are discharged before the date set for the various increases and benefits, should not have those benefits made retroactive? If they make proper application, it seems to me they should be included.
If the benefits and allowances were too low before, they are still too low for men and women whose applications have come in before the deadline. I cannot understand why they should not be treated the same as men and women who have applied after the deadline.
Much has been said in connection with the setting up of the organization. Some hon. members have suggested that the personnel of the board should consist of returned men, both from the last war and from the present war. This suggestion I heartily support, because the mature judgment of the older men will be most useful when combined with the more recently acquired knowledge of the younger men.
The new department will be faced with many problems. It will have many decisions to make, and I urge that they be made promptly. This is a point I cannot emphasize too strongly. Much of the unrest which has occurred has been due to delays. All hon. members know about the suffering which has been caused through delays in the handling of pension applications. I realize that some of these delays are unavoidable, but carelessness and inefficiency should not be tolerated.
May I refer to one or two matters which have been discussed, and which will no doubt be discussed later in connection with the payment of pensions to the returned men. I press now for a reasonable clothing allowance. The first allowance was set at $35, and it has now been increased to $65. I say that $125 is not too much for any men who have to refit themselves. Not only do they have to secure civilian clothing, but in addition they have to [DOT]obtain working clothes. I would ask any hon.
member to try to refit himself, even for $125. Certainly that figure is low enough, and undoubtedly $65 is entirely inadequate.
We note that an order in council has been issued by the government, indicating that it has yielded to pressure from members of the House of Commons, and public opinion. Pay and allowances according to rank are to be allowed for one year, two years, or more if necessary, for hospitalization. This is to date back only to May 1, 1943. I am wondering why that date was set. If the allowance originally made was too small, and if the principle was wrong after May 1, 1943, why was it not wrong and the allowance too small before that date?
All hon. members who have spoken in the debate have urged that every effort must be made to see to it that upon discharge the men are given every opportunity to get jobs.
I should like to ask in passing, the meaning of these words as they appear in earlier and very important legislation:
A man shall be reinstated in a position not worse than that he would have been in if he had not enlisted.	'
These are fine words, but what do they mean? Is it possible to reinstate a man under those circumstances? Can that be enforced?
I say it is necessary for the government before long to give us a definition of just what they mean by that wording. There is no use in keeping it there if it is just a bit of camouflage. There should be an accurate definition, so that the men will know exactly what it means, and what they may expect. At the present time they do not know what to expect, and I have heard many complaints in this regard.
Some of our men will have been out of a job, and in the army, for three, four, or possibly five or six years. Some of them never had a job. I believe it is the view of all hon. members that they should be given a proper opportunity to refit themselves for civilian life.
Why does the government propose to pay the men less while they are training for peacetime occupations than they were paid to prepare themselves to fight? It takes one or two years to train a man for warfare; yet these men who are coming back and who will have to train themselves for civilian life are expected to refit themselves and to become good citizens for less pay than they received' while they were in the army. That also' applies to their dependents. Besides, the training will probably extend over a shorter period'. This does not add up. If it was good policy to give pay and allowances while they were training to fight, certainly it is good policy to
Department of Veterans' Affairs

pay them equally well while they are fitting themselves to play their part in the kind of life for which they fought overseas. If these men are treated properly it will mean a great saving in money later. We must not be picayune now.
There are many other matters I shall discuss when the opportunity arises, but on this occasion I shall not take up more of the time of the house. I support the principle of the bill. As I said before, we should have had a department of this kind long ago.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as other hon. members have said, this is a very important measure. It establishes a Department of Veterans' Affairs, and puts in the hands of the minister of that department almost everything concerning not only men who have returned from the last war, but also those who will return from this one. We all realize that winning the war is our first task, but the rehabilitation and reconstruction period after the war is also very *important. No greater responsibility faces [DOT]the Canadian people at home to-day than to .see that the armed forces when they return get a square deal, and nothing that we can do to mssist them in those post-war days will be any [DOT]more than what is due to them and what they have earned many times over.
I am sure the house will agree that since 1914-18 no subject has been treated with more unanimity among all parties in the house than tthe problems of the veterans. Those problems have always been beyond the scope of party politics, and I am sure we are all looking at this measure with only one thought in mind, namely, to do what is right and just for our men when they return.
If this new department is wisely directed- and I think it will be because I presume the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) will be the new minister-it will be of great service to the men of the last war and also to the men returning from this war. Some of the members who have spoken in this debate have mentioned the deal that was handed out to the veterans of 1914-18. I am one of those who have always thought-and I have so expressed myself-that the veterans of 1914-18 should have been given a better deal. I have not hesitated to say so on many occasions, and I refer particularly to the veterans who settled on the land. May I recall to you, Mr. Speaker, that even last session, in speaking on the budget on March 15, I repeated a suggestion that I had made on previous occasions, that the debts of the soldier settlers on the XMr. Douglas G. Ross.]
land should be written off. I am going to quote what I said on that occasion. I said at page 1238 of Hansard:
For years I have consistently urged in this house that if the government had written off the debt arising from soldier settlement in respect of the last war, the country would have saved money. I advocate that, as part of the proposed debt adjustment, the soldier settlers' debts be written off. After all, this concession would do no more than repay these men in some small measure for what they are doing in the present war. Their sons were the first to enlist and their daughters have followed

they are in the army too.
Many of the veterans of the last war have joined up in this war. If the policy I have consistently advocated had been pursued it would have been more just, more fair and would have saved the country money.
Undoubtedly the members of the armed forces when they return will demand the right to have an opportunity to earn a decent living and to make their own way on a just and equitable basis. As other hon. members have said in this debate, the men who are fighting our battles to-day overseas-and some of them are already returning from Italy are not looking for charity or pity. All they want is a square deal. They want a chance to resume their life work, to follow perhaps the course which the war interrupted in some university, or to take up vocational training of some kind. All they want is a fair chance to fit themselves to earn a decent living, and that is certainly no more than their due.
The question of pensions both old and new has been discussed in this debate. Pensions will be the responsibility of the minister who is appointed to this department. Too often in recent years the applicant for a pension has been treated with doubt, if not distrust. The burden of proof has rested on the applicant. All that should be reversed1 by this new department and the burden of proof rest, not on the applicant to prove his case, but on the department to prove that the applicant is not entitled to pensions.
