speechtext:
Department of Veterans' Affairs
them intelligently as to the plans being formulated by this government to take care of their boys and girls when they return; I have also been able to advise the wives of men overseas as to the opportunities of rehabilitation for their husbands. So that this is indeed an important measure, and one which, if carried through upon the lines suggested, will be well received by all the people of the dominion.
I was interested in the very fine approach made to this question by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). He dealt with the subject in the broad manner in which he always approaches such questions. I was also interested in the references made by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). I was pleased that he brought the attention of the house to the case of William Hall, a coloured gentleman from Nova Scotia who was the first man in North America to win the Victoria Cross. I am thoroughly familiar with the case, and was delighted, having already put the story on the record on a previous occasion, as was also done by the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) some time ago, to have so full an account of this brave man's deed placed on Hansard in so eloquent a manner by the hon. member for Royal. I agree with what he said, and I support his suggestion that some society, the Historic Sites Society or some other, should undertake to erect at or near Windsor a tribute of respect to this brave man who has gone to the great beyond. Possibly the hon. member for Royal is not aware that we have in Halifax a branch of the Canadian Legion named after this hero- the A) illiam Hall, V.C. No. 57 branch, composed entirely of coloured men. It was my privilege and honour when that organization was first formed to provide them with a flag known as their legion flag. The branch is composed of some of our finest types of citizens- coloured men, certainly, nevertheless true and loyal and willing to do their utmost to bring about the victory and the peace for which we all hope.
I was surprised at a remark made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) when he was asking that additional employment offices or selective service offices and welfare offices be opened throughout Nova Scotia. I am in accord with this proposal, but his reference to Halifax, the capital of Nova Scotia, was a little out of place. He made the statement that Halifax is situated in the extreme western end of the province. I sincerely hope that he has not created the impiession that we are located somewhere down in the woods. Halifax, as he must know, and as the minister well knows, is at about the centre of the province; it is the logical
TMr. Isnor.]
place for the welfare office. If it is decided to establish additional offices, that is fine, but we do not want the minister or his department to do anything which would deprive us of the Halifax welfare office, which is so efficiently operated by Colonel Mackenzie, D.S.O. To prove my point let me give some figures as regards distances. From Yarmouth to Sydney, that is, from one end of the province to the district which the hon. member for Cape Breton South represents, is 538 miles. From Sydney to Halifax is 288 miles, and from Yarmouth to Halifax, 250 miles; so that it will be seen that we have a central location so far as the welfare office is concerned. While Halifax is the logical place for the welfare office, we have a very fine type of man looking after the returned soldiers, a man who has been an outstanding figure in veterans' affairs in Nova Scotia. He is well-known to practically every ex-serviceman who served in the last war, and he has already made himself well known to a large number of those who are serving in the present war.
I rose more particularly to express my approval of the general principle of the bill. I will not refer to any particular clause or clauses. They have been already dealt with, and in my opinion the proper time to consider them in specific detail is when the sections come before the committee of the whole. I endorse, and I feel that the people will endorse, the general principle of the bill, but I would bring to the attention of the minister this consideration. I feel that the men who are serving at the present time-and the same goes for the women-are not familiar enough with the benefits that will accrue from this measure. In my opinion every one of them should receive a pamphlet of some kind outlining the benefits of the measure, the rehabilitation grants which will be provided, the scheme of vocational training, the medical treatment to which they will be entitled, pensions, the plan for soldier settlement and the efforts that are being made to take care of their future employment and reestablishment in civilian life. With that thought in mind I bring to the attention of the house, as I understand the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) did on a previous occasion, a very fine book which I purchased in a book store. I was not as fortunate as the hon. member, for I did not receive a copy with the author's compliments, but this is an excellent book entitled, "When the Boys Come Home", written by C. N. Senior. It is a book that everyone will enjoy reading. It is easy reading and is very informative. If this book or a similar one could be placed in the hands of every member of the armed forces

Department of Veterans' Affairs
it would do much to satisfy them about their future welfare. More than that, I believe that the parents and members of the families of those serving should also read the book. It would show them what the government is trying to do for the members of the armed forces.
I will not go into details, but I might say in passing that the book touches upon a variety of interesting topics such as the postdischarge reestablishment order, Veterans' Land Act, historical background, pensions, hospitals, medical care, time of discharge, the boys in the merchant navy, and so on. The whole thing is well written, and the interesting point about it is that the author's royalties are pledged to the disablement fund. In other words, this well known official of the Department of Pensions and National Health, in his own time, has written a very fine book which I suggest should be placed in the hands of all members of the armed forces.
I desire to bring to the attention of the house one matter which I regard as very important, namely, the treatment of totally disabled veterans. I am sure every hon. member knows of some particular case, but I do not propose to deal with a number of complaints. We are bound to get complaints. When I first became a federal member I was besieged with requests to have cases reopened. It is hard to establish continuity in many cases. I went into these cases and, like other members, I have a file, not an inch or two inches, but many inches high, dealing with different cases. I could quote, as did the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), individual cases, but I do not think this is the proper place to do that.
I have had satisfaction from the officials of the department. Any cases that I have brought to their notice they have carefully considered and have taken the trouble to point out to me wherein certain cases did not come within the terms of the regulations, and as gracefully as I could I accepted the decision. I went back several times to make sure that no point was overlooked, and I always found them very willing to make a full review of cases in an effort to see that justice was done.
I said that I was anxious to bring this matter before the minister and to discuss the question of totally disabled veterans. I do not think I can do so better than by dealing with one individual case. The one to which I refer is well known to seventy-five per cent of Nova Scotians. It is known to a very large number of men and women who are serving overseas at the present time, because of the
activities of the gentleman in question on behalf of those persons. He personally supervises the sending of 125,000 cigarettes every month. Through his efforts millions of cigarettes have gone overseas. When I describe this man to hon. members they will realize that the request I make to the minister in this public way should receive his sympathetic attention.
I have in mind one who has suffered for something like fourteen years, and I have committed to writing the thoughts I have in this regard. When I think of those who are prone to complain, my thoughts turn to a veteran of the last war and compare his attitude with that of those who complain. The veteran to whom I refer is Walter Callow, known as "the human log," a patient at Camp Hill hospital, Halifax. This man exemplifies in true fashion the virtue of patience so well shown in the Bible story relating to Job's afflictions. Callow, as before mentioned, is a veteran of the first great war. He was injured in an airplane crash. He is well known to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of National Defence for Air, and also the Minister of Pensions and National Health, who have all at one time or another visited this veteran at Camp Hill hospital. I have on many occasions called to see him and I wish I could1 depict to you, sir, in fitting terms the spirit of this man, the frame of mind and the cheerful greeting which he extends to his many visitors. Think of a man who has lain in bed for fourteen years, unable to move or turn; his arms and legs are twisted, he cannot move them; his neck is as stiff as steel. He cannot move his jaws, and now he is also blind. While he cannot turn his head he seems to know the footstep of every visitor. His mind is ever working, planning things to do to help our veteran soldiers, writing poetry on cards, raffling this and that to buy cigarettes for boys now serving overseas. With this picture in mind I just wish to recall that I knew him as a boy who played hockey games, who took his bumps, and it made no difference how big they came, they always found him tough. Do you think he complains about controls and restrictions? No, he never complains.
I have photographs of this man here which I wish I could pass around to hon. members so that they could see how deformed every joint is, and how they are out of shape. It is this man that I am asking the minister to bear in mind when he is building new hospitals throughout Canada and when he is building that fine new addition which he has promised

Department of Veterans' Affairs
to Halifax, as an extension to the present Camp Hill hospital. I am asking him to provide suitable quarters in a separate portion of the building for this man who from day to day is compelled to lie and suffer. I am asking him to provide this accommodation so that this man may have some quietness of mind and that comfort by orderlies may be extended to him to make his remaining days just a little easier.
In conclusion, I hope the minister in his sympathetic way will take this into consideration when building future hospitals and particularly see if arrangements can be made whereby this veteran will enjoy the privacy of a small place that he can call his own and not have to wait for a new hospital.

speechtext:
I am
sure the minister must feel highly gratified at the unanimity with which bill No. 83 has been received from all corners of the house. I am not rising to discuss the bill at any length. As other speakers have done, I wish to register my support of the bill. Had I not received two or three letters recently-one of them to-day-I would take my seat after having made these few remarks in order that the bill could get into committee more quickly and through the house. However, I am not going to apologize for speaking even briefly on this bill. Like the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who is known throughout the country as the soldier's friend, I in my time have had to do with a large number of soldiers following the last war. The section of the city of Toronto that I have the honour to represent sent a large number of soldiers overseas. It is true that the hon. member for Broadview received a title that so far as I know no one else in Canada received. It wras conferred on him by royalty and none other than the present Duke of Windsor, who was Prince of Wales at that time. His Royal Highness visited Toronto immediately following the end of the war, and during the term of the hon. member for Broadview who was mayor of Toronto for seven years. At that time he conferred on the hon. member the title of "the soldier's friend." He richly deserved it for the service he had rendered to the soldiers. I left a life of what would have been leisure at that time to come here to serve the soldiers, having had so much to do with them following the last war, at which time I was president of the British Imperial

association, as I had been during the war. That is a title I have always been proud of; it is a great organization.
When I heard the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) say last night that this bill conferred wide powers on the minister I said to myself, I am glad to hear it. Quite frankly everybody in the house may not be glad, but on various occasions when I have spoken to the minister about certain veterans he has said to me, " If I had the power I would see that that man received redress." On many occasions I have heard that from the late chairman of the pension commission, General Macdonald. I happened to be in Banff on the day he died or the day after. In any event I went to pay my respects to Mrs. Macdonald. The body was not in view at that time. I should like to say here and now that this country was never served by a more sympathetic commissioner or chairman than the late General Macdonald. On many occasions he said to me, " If I had the power and was not circumscribed by those regulations I would grant relief." Therefore I am hoping that the minister, now having that power, will be able to transfer it to the new chairman, whom I have always found very sympathetic, and that is what one would expect from a man who comes from Glasgow, Scotland, the land of the minister. Therefore I am looking for great things from the minister since he has the power that the hon. member for Vancouver South referred to in his able speech last night. It was one of the best speeches delivered in this house in this debate. It was delivered in his usual capable way.
I am not going to deal with the whole of the bill but with section 7, paragraph (g). I think it covers, what I wish to bring up. Section 7 reads:
(1) Subject to the approval of the governor in council, the minister may make such regulations, from time to time, as he may deem necessary and advisable.
I am glad the minister has the power. He is a returned soldier himself. I have always found him sympathetic to returned men. I hope the cases I shall mention will receive his special consideration. Paragraph (g) of section 7 reads:
for the payment of pensions out of moneys provided by parliament for the purpose to persons who, while rendering service to Canada in the prosecution of any war, suffer any injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death not otherwise pensionable or to the dependents of such persons. ,
Under that section I desire to mention one case of the present war. This is a letter I received from Sergeant R. Haire, of 19 Afton avenue, Toronto. I might say that in that

Department of Veterans' Affairs
part of the city of Toronto there are two men who are of the type that render eminent service to returned soldiers. I really do not know what this country would be like without men such as the man to whom this letter refers, Thomas Baldwin, and another gentleman around the corner on Northcote avenue, by the name of Truman Meriam, also a returned soldier. Both men are the type of men to whom people in distress go, and they are never turned down. So the Thomas Baldwin referred to in this letter is the man I have just described:
Dear Sir,
I have recently returned home from overseas, and I was in a quandary as to what I should do in order to get compassionate leave, and of course I got in touch with Thomas Baldwin, whom I have known for this past ten years, who immediately wrote to you

Being in my riding, of course they write to me.
-and explained my case, and in return I received a reply from you.
You stated in your letter that I should make out an application form for my release, which I did, and up until now I have had no word as to whether I am going to get this release or not. X was overseas for the last four and a half years, in which time the little cartage business I had has practically become extinct, and of course I would like to build up this business so as I could have something to return to whenever this war is over.
That is all I need read from that letter. This man's address is 19 Afton avenue, and what I have read will appear in Hansard. I should like to ask the minister whether he will have any power, through some of the ramifications of his big, new department, to assist a man like this to start up some little business such as he had before the war? That question need not be answered now; the minister can give me the information at another time.
The next letter I wish to read is from a returned soldier who served in the last war, who I believe was overseas for four years or more. I have taken up this case with the department many times, and this man has been here to see the department officials, whom he found, as I have always found them, to be courteous, considerate and sympathetic, but who under the present arrangement do not appear to 'have the authority which the minister will now have. Therefore I bring this man's case to his attention in the hope that when he reviews it some way will be found to help this man. This man, William Robertson, No. 534262, also was born in Scotland, I believe somewhere near Glasgow; his brogue is so good it is hard to understand
him, and he always signs himself "Scotty".
I know the minister will give fair play to everyone, of every race, and I only mention in passing that this man is from the old country. He has been in Christie Street hospital several times, and I have seen him in the most distressing circumstances. The last time I saw him he was in a very distressed state, but he has not been able to get more than a small pension, which I believe amounts to $22 a month. In fairness to the department I must say that they offered to put him on veterans' allowance, but he is a man of the sternest principles. He feels that if his physical condition is such that he is entitled also to the equivalent of veterans' allowance he is entitled to pension of that amount extra, and he feels that the only honourable way he can accept pension is for disabilities received in the war. I wrote asking for the name of his doctor, and in reply he says:
Sorry for delay in answering your letter. Just got over severe vomiting spell.
I have seen him vomiting very severely, when I would not have been surprised if he had passed out in his distress.
Well, Doctor Smith's address is Doctor Orminston Smith, 3 Regal road, corner of Regal road and Oakwood avenue, Toronto. No operation for the present. Strict ulcer diet- medicine-sunshine-complete rest and quietness. So I am leaving for Wasaga beach; a friend of mine has a cottage there. So I am going there to beat the white corpuscles, the reds are on the weak side.
I suppose that is a medical term; the white corpuscles destroy the red ones.
But the reds will win out when old man sunshine gets after them, and I hope to come up stronger than ever.
I have known this man for years. For reasons I am not going to mention there has been some conflict between him and the department, but then everyone cannot present his case in the nicest way. I have always found this man very reasonable, and I am going to ask the minister to have his case especially reviewed. If he is entitled to war veterans' allowance, why not increase his pension? Certainly his physical condition is such that if something is not done he cannot live very long.
I should like to mention one more case which I have taken up with the department many times. It is the case of George Stevens, 416 Salem avenue, Toronto, whose regimental number was 57727. This man draws a pension of $20. Some days ago I wrote Mr. Stevens asking him to restate his case, so that when the proper time came I might present it to the
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

minister and the house, and I am taking advantage of this opportunity to do so. He writes:
I enlisted in Toronto on November 11, 1914. I landed in France in September, 1915. I was gassed in April, 1916, by shell gas at Kemal and was sent down the line to Etaples, No. 18 general hospital, where I was for sis weeks. Instead of me going on leave to England, which was due me, I was sent up t'he line again into the Ypres salient and in less than a week the action took place, on the 2nd of June in Ypres, where I was taken prisoner. The Germans lined me up with several more to shoot us

I might digress here to say that I have heard him tell how he was lined up in the trench with some of his fellows after having been taken out of a dug-out. I doubt if any human being can picture the agony a man would be going through watching other men lining up ready to shoot him.
[DOT]-but a German field marshal came along and intervened and told the guards to take us prisoners. Through the terrible mental ordeal I went through carrying four of our own wounded men out under our own shell fire. The German doctor at our dressing station commended me for my courage but said I was badly shell shocked. This doctor asked me to take off my tunic; he held one end and I held the other; we wrung it out and the perspiration rolled out of it as though it had been in the river, through this mental agony under fire. I was kept behind the lines for three days carrying out wounded men, and ammunition up to the line under our own heavy shell fire; and then we started our march into Germany which took three days, with the Uhlans as our guards, driving us along until we reached the first prison camp, Dulman, where we lived for the first six months on black bread and watery soup, until the food packages came through.
I presume he means packages from Canada.
Our next move was to a munition factory in Munster, -where we refused to work on munitions, so they punished us by putting us in a detention camp and then taking us into a large room where they put high pressure steam on, [DOT] with very little ventilation. Our clothes were taken away from us and we were in there for forty-eight hours on a diet of water. The air was so humid the perspiration just oozed out of us. When we came out we were almost too weak to stand. We wrere also clubbed with the butt of a rifle on several occasions. We were beaten with a rubber pipe. Our next move was to Minden where we worked in the camp and on the roads. We were there for about four months. Our last move was to Friedrichs-feld where we -worked in the coal mines for nineteen months. We were maltreated there many times. The innocent had to suffer for the guilty, for if one prisoner done any wrong you were all punished. This punishment was standing in the pouring rain with your hands above your head for so many minutes, and then in another position with your hands outstretched for so long that you had not dare bat an eyebrow or the sentry would butt you in the back with his rifle butt. We were released three weeks after November 11, 1918.

Now, just a word. I do not think any physician could possibly accurately diagnose the disability accruing from the distress suffered by a soldier under those conditions. It is a very difficult picture to describe. I present to the minister this case, one which the former chairman had before him on many occasions-That chairman is not here now, but he called me on the telephone at one time, asking me to tell Mr. Stevens that he was going to see that his pension was increased, as it should have been. Later, however, when it was not raised he informed me that because of the regulations he could not increase 'it. Had he lived I am sure he would have found some way to make the increase. Now that the minister has the power described by the hon. member for Vancouver South, I hope that this case, and the other one I mentioned, will come under his personal review.
I have had long contact with Mr. Stevens, and I can say that at times I have seen him in conditions of the utmost distress, almost unable to breathe. I have seen him sitting at the edge of the sidewalk, because of his heart condition. I cannot understand why a condition of that kind would not show up upon investigation. Some things have been found wrong, because he has been given a certain amount of pension, although not very much.
With the presentation of these cases I have completed what I wish to say at this time. May I compliment the minister upon the introduction of the bill; the whole house is behind it. With the new authority he now has-and I do not like to see him shaking his head, because I am taking the word of the hon. member for Vancouver South who, on nooccasion, would exaggerate-

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this measure, which is based on a principle of justice and a feeling of gratitude, is most timely. I believe it should be passed and carried out at once..

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
It certainly behooves the authorities and the people of this country to give serious thought to ensuring the reestablishment of veterans and the care of the wounded after the war, when the time comes to demobilize all those stout-hearted men who are now fighting in. defence of an ideal. But it often happens that the w'orst measures are applied with the utmost strictness. On the other hand, measures that are infinitely better are applied neither so effectively nor with so much eagerness. Ever since the beginning of the war, that is in 1939 and 1940, when a campaign of voluntary enlistments was launched, we have heard members of the government and many people in Canada state that after the war on the return of those young men who had been called upon to uphold our cause on the battlefields, action would be taken with a view to ensuring them a better treatment than was given to the veterans of the great war, who were not, as we readily admit, treated as they should have been. I wish to quote, as an illustration, a case where that promise was not immediately implemented. In 1941, the veterans from the city of Quebec, organized into an association, requested me to point out to you and to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) the serious grounds for complaint which they had in Quebec. Those veterans, after two years of war. could not *obtain employment in arsenals. They claimed to be the victims of political _ discrimination and they voiced many other complaints of a rather serious nature. Following a pretty sharp debate with the Minister of National Defence, a board of inquiry was sent to Quebec with instructions to deal with those complaints. Its work had very good results. Such an incident shows that, two years after promises had been made to the men who are fighting in this war, no thought had been given to the matter of a fair treatment for the veterans of the last war. Therefore, I hope that we shall not be satisfied with making speeches, drafting an act and writing it into the statute books, but that the kindly feelings we entertain will move us to action, that this very necessary legislation which has the approval of everyone to-day, may find an echo in our minds and hearts, and be carried out at once.
(Text)
Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the capital Importance of this bill, I have been asked by Jubilee branch, No. 59, of the Canadian legion of the British empire service league, Gaspe, Quebec, to bring to your attention and to that of the proper authority in the house a matter which is of direct concern to the veterans. The following letter will explain the whole matter:
Gaspe, County Gaspe,
Quebec,
May 9, 1944.
Mr. J. S. Roy,
M.P. for Gaspe,
Parliament Building,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Roy:-
Major deGruchy of Cape-Cove, who is a member of this lodge, has sent us a copy of a letter which you sent him, from Mr. Macdonald, Parliamentary Assistant, to the Minister of National Defence, regarding the Canadian volunteer service ribbon.
In fairness to all who served whether for one or eighteen months, we, members of this lodge, feel that this matter should be brought to the attention of the ministers of national defence, and we would deem it a great favour if you, as our representative, would bring this matter to the attention of the house.
We are enclosing copy of an article which we are sending to the legion at Ottawa, and also a resolution from this lodge asking that in fairness to all those who volunteered and served and who were, for medical reasons or otherwise honourably discharged, that they be entitled to this ribbon as all volunteers who served eighteen months or more. These men who were not fortunate enough to complete this length of service showed their willingness by volunteering to serve their country in the time of need, and therefore, the least the Department of National Defence can do is to award this ribbon to all who volunteered, and make no distinction as to length of service. We trust that your representation may be the means of having this rectified.
We feel that we can safely say that anything which you may be able to do regarding this will be greatly appreciated by all concerned. Thanking you for your kindness, I remain, Yours respectfully,
Reg. R. deGruchy, Captn., President Jubilee branch, No. 59, Canadian Legion.
I am pleased to say that I have had the cooperation of the parliamentary assistant of the Minister of National Defence, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Macdonald), who has devoted a great deal of his time in the course of two weeks in helping me straighten out this matter and to bring justice and satisfaction to these volunteers for active service who have been discharged for reasons of health. I should like to put on the record his letter to me dated Ottawa, June 6, 1944:
J. S. Roy, Esq., M.P.,
647 House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Roy,
Re: Canadian Volunteer Service Medal I am now informed that the question of amplifying the eligibility provisions of governing order in council to include persons of any rank who have voluntarily served on active war service and have been honourably discharged or retired as a result of injury or disease or aggravation thereof, attributable to
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

or lncurred during such active war service, is under active consideration at the present time.
I understand that the proposed extension contemplates persons honourably discharged for medical reasons and the question of awarding the medal to personnel of less than eighteen months' service honourably discharged for other reasons is not now under active consideration.
I think this will give you all the information that you need in order to answer the inquiries of the Jubilee branch (Gaspe) of the Canadian legion.
Yours truly,
W. C. Macdonald, Parliamentary Assistant.
There is a ray of hope, but it looks to me is though a long time will elapse before satisfaction is given to these volunteers who have been discharged for honourable reasons, such as their condition of health. I again ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) to comply with the request of these volunteers who have shown earnestness and willingness to serve their country. They are entitled to recognition of the attitude which they took at the beginning of the war, the same as those who are still serving at the present time.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
I do not intend to deal at any length with the bill now before the house. The minister has one thing in his favour; he comes from British Columbia and therefore he should know something of what he is doing.
I believe I can indicate my attitude to the bill in .general by saying that I thoroughly endorse practically everything that has been said during this debate by Liberal, Conservative, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and Social Credit members. I wish, however, to reiterate one or two points to which I think more attention should be paid by the minister, especially in his new department.
A reference was made by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) to the attitude of the treasury board in connection with the claims of returned soldiers. It is a position which I have never been able to understand. I believe that the government would be well advised, particularly in view of some of the things which have taken place in the last forty-eight hours, to take measures whereby more members, if not all the members, of the board which handles any matters connected with soldiers shall be themselves returned men. I have every respect for the members of the treasury board. I do not know who they all are; I do not know what they are for; I do not believe they always know themselves what they are for; but I think the veterans are entitled to better consideration from them, particularly in view

of what has been said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as to what we as Canadian citizens owe our returned men.
I would particularly impress upon the minister that in the past the whole onus of proving the veteran's case has been placed on the veteran. I saw the minister shake his head this afternoon when the statement was made by one hon. member, but it cannot be denied. I agree with a statement made this afternoon, which probably has been repeated by other hon. members who have spoken with reference to this bill, that if a man is accepted for service as A-l, he should be the government's responsibility in the category of A-l from the time they take him into the army and for all future time.
Another suggestion I would make to the minister is that he eliminate red tape. As a member of the legion, and having been interested for many years in veterans' affaire, I know it requires a lawyer to understand the Pension Act and much of the other legislation having to do with returned soldiers. I am sure the minister is interested in doing everything possible to simplify all that concerns the veterans. It should not be necessary for them to have an advocate every time they approach a departmental official.
When the bill is in committee I should like to speak in some detail on the Veterans' Land Act, the subject in which I am particularly interested. Coming from British Columbia and from a large rural riding in that province,
I am naturally more interested in the land act than in any other portion of the bill which has been so well discussed in this chamber, especially by hon. members who themselves are ex-servicemen. I do not believe that the Veterans' Land Act in its present form is of any value, at least in the lower part of British Columbia on mixed farms. In my opinion, which is endorsed by every organization I know of, from boards of trade down, in the Fraser Valley, it is absolutely impossible for a soldier, no matter what his training or his knowledge of agriculture, to start operations and look after his family, meet ordinary living costs, let alone pay any principal and interest, if he has only $1,200 worth of stock on a mixed farm. I believe that any agriculturist will bear me out in that contention. If the government wants to make the act effective, at least in the Fraser Valley and the lower mainland of British Columbia, it must give consideration to a larger grant for stock and equipment. Further the government have reserved some 700 Japanese farms for the men who are coming back. I am sorry that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is not in his

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
place, because this is more his responsibility than that of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). It is out of the question for any veteran to settle on a strawberry or raspberry farm-that is what they all are-so long as he allows some bureaucrat who does not know a strawberry from a toadstool to set the price of these berries. I hope the Minister of Pensions and National Health will be the soldier's friend when it comes to endeavouring to put some pressure on the minister who is responsible in this connection.
I turn now to another matter. As I have said, I endorse practically everything which has been said by all hon. members in connection with the bill, and shall have more to say about it when it is in committee. I did not happen to be in the house last night; I was on other business with my room-mate, who has left to join his unit. I had the privilege during the two years he was overseas of looking after his riding; and we were checking over files and various matters which he wishes me to look after now that he is returning to active service. But I have discovered that an hon. gentleman with a wonderful military record took occasion to make an attack on my room-mate and colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver North. He also made some remarks about myself. I am not worrying over what he said about myself; he has said these things a few times before, and any time the hon. member for Temiscouata says anything about the member for Fraser Valley, Cruickshank gets some more votes. I should like to read a letter I have received from one of the most prominent members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party in British Columbia. It is dated from Hatzic, April 27. This warrior friend of mine from Temiscouata has some favourite expressions which he likes to level at the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and Barclay's bank and the civil servants; he also likes to tell me that I wall not be re-elected. But here is the letter from Hatzic:
Dear George:
I have just read a couple of clippings in a Vancouver paper, which I enclose. I certainly approve of the method you have of addressing such men as herein indicated, J. F. Pouliot, for instance. You surely let them all know B.C. can speak for itself. The Speaker evidently knows his business too.
And this part I should like to bring to the notice of the hon. member who says to each member he does not like, "You won't be elected." I want him to hear this line from a past president of the C.C.F. association in my riding:
The next election may also prove Pouliot to he a false prophet.
So that I am not particularly worried about what the hon. member for Temiscouata may have said about myself last night or at any other time. The more he says, the more certain I am of being returned to Ottawa.
I think every hon. member will give me credit for the fact that I do not often either follow notes or read anything, but in order that there may be no misunderstanding about this I want to follow my notes fairly carefully.
I should like to turn now to the cowardly attack made by the hon. member for Temiscouata on the hon. member for Vancouver North. I say "cowardly" advisedly, for the hon. member waited until the hon. member for Vancouver North had left the house to return to his duties in the Royal Canadian Air Force before he made his slur. If the hon. member for Vancouver North were here he would be able to take care of himself.
That there might be no mistake to-day, I wrote the hon. member for Temiscouata, as follows:
Ottawa, Ontario,
June 16, 1944.
Mr. J. F. Pouliot, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, On-t.
Sir:	. [DOT]
As I intend making reference to yourself in the house during the day, as a matter ol courtesy I am waiting you to this eiiect m order that you may, should you so desire, be present during my remarks.
I want it to be perfectly clear that I never say anything that I am afraid to say in front of a man; I never have done so and I never will. I want to quote the facts about the hon. member for Vancouver North because I want them to be accurate. The hon. member enlisted as aircrew on September 4, 1939, but because of his age he was not called up until the spring of 1940. He was then called as an administrative officer rather than as aircrew because the services felt that with his training he would be of more value in such capacity.
He bitterly resented this and attempted to remuster as a navigator in the fall of 1940 but was turned down on medical grounds as unfit for tropical service, which is amusing in view of his later service in the desert. He went overseas in 1940 and served with two Canadian fighter squadrons as adjutant. When the Royal Air Force raised the age for aircrew he applied and was accepted for aircrew, but this was stopped by the Royal Canadian Air Force. He then volunteered for service in Libya, reverting from squadron leader to flight lieutenant in order to do so.
He served from Alamein to Tunis, then in Malta, and he was the first Canadian airman to wade ashore from a barge in the invasion of Sicily. Yet he is referred to as a penguin by the warrior of Temiscouata. All any hon.
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

member need to do is to ask any airman what he thinks of Flight Lieutenant Jimmy Sinclair. They need only read Hansard of the past two days to see the many fine things which have been said by members of all parties about his efforts in the house for his comrades in the service.
Now let us examine the military record of the hon. member for Temiscouata. According to the Parliamentary Guide, which is issued to every hon. member, the hon. member for Temiscouata was born in 1890. On August 4, 1914 he would have been twenty-four years of age and in 1918 he would have been twenty-eight years of age. That is, during the last war his age would range from twenty-four to twenty-eight years. As an old soldier I know that is the ideal age at which to be a soldier. The Parliamentary Guide shows no record of service in the first great war. _
According to Hansard the record of service of the hon. member in the second great war would appear to be to discourage the enlistment of farmers' sons and in no way to have encouraged the purchase of victory bonds to buy supplies for a gift to battered Britain. He has done more than anyone else to hurt the [DOT]cause of unity by putting Quebec before the eyes of the rest of Canada in a light which in no way is the due of a province that produced the famous Twenty-Second Battalion, a unit which I had the honour to serve alongside in the first great war. No; the hon. member for Temiscouata who fights so courageously against civil servants or members of the armed forces who cannot fight back is not in a position to know what a slit trench in the bombed desert means, to know of sleepless nights on the sands, to live on iron rations, to share with his comrades the cruelties of war. How could he when he has never seen war, never known war other than that of endless speeches with an eye always on the battle front of the Temiscouata elections.
Unfortunately the rest of Canada judge the great province of Quebec by the utterances of such men as the hon. member for Temiscouata. When I go home to my riding,
I am not asked, "What is the price of milk? What have you done about farm labour?" I am asked, and I am sure many other members from western Canada are also asked, "What are you going to do about Quebec?" I want to say to hon. members from Quebec that it is extremely unfortunate that their spokesman is apparently the hon. member for Temiscouata. I know he does not express the feelings of many fine members from the province of Quebec. Every time I go back home I defend the province of Quebec.

Quebec is a wonderful province and has made a great contribution, not only to the present war but to the last war. But unfortunately such men as this broadcast their remarks across Canada as representing the soul of Quebec. I do not think it is the soul of Quebec to call an airman who volunteered in 1939 a penguin when he served throughout the Africa-Sicily campaign, to call him a penguin when one son of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) is serving as adjutant of the squadron in which the hon. member for Vancouver North served. Another son of the minister is a prisoner in Hong Kong, and yet this so-called spokesman for Quebec calls my room-mate, a soldier in this war like Flight Lieutenant James Sinclair, the hon. member for Vancouver North, a penguin.
I want to tell the hon. member for Temiscouata that I think I speak not only for my province but for all members in this house when I say that they bow their heads with shame that any member shoidd defame a fighting man from Africa and Sicily by calling him a penguin.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the placing of veterans' affairs under a separate department is not only acceptable to the men of the armed forces but I know it will be very desirable to the administration especially when these men are returning from overseas in greater numbers. The bill makes provision for the care and training of veterans, especially disabled veterans who, I take it for granted, will be cared for and treated under the Department of Veterans' Affairs. I assume also that the blind veterans will come under the care and direction of the Canadian national institute for the blind. Certainly they could get no better care. I notice that one section of the bill gives the minister direction and control over the workshops of the institute in which the blind will be trained, but I take it that there will be an arrangement made between the Canadian national institute and the administration.
There is not much that can be said on this bill without repetition, and the debate has been a series of repetitions. In the regulations issued under a recent order and which became effective on June 1, reference was made to the members of the forces who served in the northwest rebellion. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has been most persistent in his plea on behalf of the members of those forces. He has asked that they be brought under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. Pensions are provided for the disabled, but unfortunately these men do not come under the benefits of this act.

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
There are not a great many of them. A man who enlisted at the youngest age of eighteen in 1885 would be seventy-seven years old to-day, so that I think it will be admitted by all hon. members that if the treasury board showed a little generosity it would not make much of a dent in the federal exchequer to permit these men to have the benefits of this act which would give a man $30 a month if he were single and $60 if married. These men were looked upon as being heroes in the days of 1885. It was a long arduous march which they made and they encountered considerable exposure. The answer made to the hon. member for Broadview was that in order for them to come under the War Veterans' Allowance Act it was necessary that they have served in a theatre of war, were sixty years of age and in necessitous circumstances.
I have had cases before the war veterans' allowance board and they were disposed of promptly according to their merits. . I had one case of a man who had not gone out of Canada and another one who had not gone any farther than England. The board very rightly said: "By no stretch of the imagination could England be considered as a theatre of war in the last war." Neither could Canada be declared a theatre of war at that time. Therefore that disposed of the contention that these men could not be granted an allowance. There was another reason given, namely, in order to accommodate these men the territory covered by the north and south shores of the Saskatchewan river where the uprising took place would have to be declared a theatre of war. It was not a theatre of war such as we know to-day. But there were four or five battles fought there and some four hundred men were wounded. There were also twenty-six killed. In the battle of Batoche fifty-one rebels were killed. The five battles are recorded in the archives. They were the battles of Frog Lake, Fish Lake, Batoche, Cut Knife and so on. There were five places in which there were encounters. Many were killed and wounded and many more suffered from exposure. Some six hundred mounted policemen joined that force. Those who were wounded were pensioned. The minister will remember that a few years ago a cash gratuity was given to the survivors, but none of them have come under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. In my own town I have three or four of those old veteran mounted policemen. There were some who were not in the police force. There were five thousand members of that force. There were infantry, cavalry and artillery forces from the cities of Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Kingston and Calgary. As I say, it
is all recorded in the archives of this country. By the way, very little of the history of the rebellion comes to the attention of readers of to-day, but correct reports are kept in the archives branch. I believe that the government would be justified-and I appeal to the minister to give thought to it-in bringing the members of the forces of the northwest rebellion within the benefits of the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
Another matter which has been mentioned in connection with this new department is that of bringing the soldier settlement board within the terms and the orbit of this act. So much has been said about it that this is one case in which there is real repetition. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) and other hon. members from all parts of the house have suggested that the indebtedness be wiped out entirely. It was a hazardous and uncertain game to start with.' Twenty-five thousand soldiers took advantage of the Soldier Settlement Act. We all know the adversities with which they were faced, so much so that thirteen thousand, according to the reports issued just prior to the outbreak of the war, had abandoned their venture entirely. A few have paid up and acquired titles. Some eight hundred had traded or disposed of their equity. But the point to remember is that many of them were able to secure reductions; as a matter of fact they all secured certain reductions. They had reductions of interest, bonus payments and so on two or three times. But there was one point that they did not all take advantage of and that is the only point on which I am going to make my plea on behalf of the soldier settlers. Many of the soldiers took advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to such an extent that fhey materially reduced their indebtedness. Far more did they reduce their indebtedness than did many who paid their principal and interest. The reason why they did not all take advantage of it was that they were not all in the same financial straits. As I said, they had paid their interest and principal and were not called upon to make a settlement; whereas the field men, in some instances at any rate, when they went around and tried to make collections from those settlers who were in arrears actually suggested that they take advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and materially reduce their indebtedness.
The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was nothing more than a method of permitting the farmers to go through bankruptcy, a method which did not apply to them until the act had been brought into force along about 1930. As I say, there were those who did

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
not pay but who took advantage of the rearrangement of their indebtedness when the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act came into the picture and they were far better off than those who paid. Therefore my one appeal to the minister, since he is taking over this new department, is to start with a cleaner sheet by putting every man on a level and allow those who have not had the benefit of reducing their indebtedness through the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to take that advantage. At the present time it applies only to Alberta and Saskatchewan, and since the end of the year to Manitoba. It should be made retroactive to British Columbia. I think it would be doing a gracious act and it would be cutting down the indebtedness of the soldiers. You would be putting them more on an even basis if you were just to all of them, and you can only be just to all of them by relieving those who did not apply for that rearrangement under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and reducing their indebtedness to the equivalent of those who benefited.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
I want to take the opportunity which this debate affords to say a word or two to the house in explanation of the organizations which have been set up in the three service departments, which organizations have to do with what we call discharge affairs. I trouble the house to listen to me in this matter because there has already been some misapprehension with regard to the office which these organizations have to fill in the service departments. I want it understood at the outset that those services which I shall describe in a moment are purely intended to be supplementary to the services which I believe, and I am sure ex-servicemen generally believe, have been so efficiently rendered by my colleague and his Department of Pensions and National Health with respect to returned men's problems. But it has seemed to some of us that there is a tendency-and this happens in connection with not only ex-servicemen's affairs but other matters as well-to separate governmental departments into [DOT]water-tight compartments and, as some of the public have flippantly described it, for one *department to "pass the buck" to another.
There is a clear line of demarcation between the objects and functions of the Department *of Pensions and National Health and those *of the three defence services represented by the Departments of National Defence for Army, Air and Naval Services. That clear line of demarcation is that theoretically and perhaps legally, the three defence departments have nothing to do with a man after he is

discharged from the defence services. From that time on the Department of Pensions and National Health takes him on, and some people might say that on this account the three defence services have nothing to do with a man who is prospectively to be discharged, because, after all, whatever is eventually to be done with respect to him must be done by the Department of Pensions and National Health.	So	that the impression	has	goneabroad	that	the appointment of	the	threeofficers	who	were mentioned in	the	press
announcement a week or so ago was in some way infringing upon the Department of Pensions and National Health. I know my colleague and his officials understand perfectly that this is not so. I want to say that there is the closest cooperation between us, and I should like this house and the country to understand that there is neither any intent to infringe nor any infringement of any kind. I have believed that instead of departments working in water-tight compartments-not, as it were, not letting the right hand know what the left hand does-it is necessary-and this applies not to departments alone but to branches of departments-that departments, instead of working on their own, should integrate, should mesh or gear into each other in their activities-I do not like the word "coordinate" so much-and that is exactly what the organization of which I shall speak in a moment is intended to do. That is, it is intended to gear into the activities of the Department of Pensions and National Health, but to do so in advance of the man leaving the service, so that he may have the benefit of a certain amount of advice, a certain amount of knowledge, a certain amount of training and a certain amount of planning by the defence services themselves, of which he is a member. In this way he may be better prepared, and have better facilities provided, to return and take up his position in civil life.
While I am speaking of the Department of Pensions and National Health, I want to remind the house that when the time comes for a man to be discharged or, even more important., when the time comes for general demobilization, you will find that there will be interested in that man not only fhe three defence services but also the Department of Pensions and National Health, which has had to do primarily with pensions and treatment of disabled men; the department of reconstruction, which will have a tremendous amount to do with the matter of providing employment, I mean by way of the conversion of war industries to civilian production-

speechtext:
Of course the department of reconstruction has not been set up, but it will have a very real job to do at least in connection with ex-service men in the mass, to provide and assist in providing employment which may be useful in helping them to return to civil life. Then there is the Department of Labour-perhaps I should have put it in the second place-which will have a great deal to do with the placement of men in various industries, subject, of course, to the right of those men to receive their old jobs back under the provisions of the legislation already in force. So that there are the armed services and these three departments particularly, and there may be others, all of which will have something to do with the ex-service man.
This is what the armed services have done. I am not going to use the word "discharged" any more than I can help, because I am not particularly enamoured of it. I like to think of the transition, shall I say, of a man from service to civilian life simply as the "changeover" from war service to peace service. Looking forward to that change-over, the defence services do not take the position that they are not concerned with a man after his discharge. Neither do they take the position that they are not concerned with the man who prospectively will be discharged. They believe that they have some duty and responsibility to him in both those aspects. The reason is that it is felt that the defence services know something about the work that man has done. He has been a member of the fighting forces which have been under the administration of these departments. He has assisted in carrying out the duties of fighting men, in carrying out the duties laid upon these departments to maintain Canada's armed forces. So that it does seem desirable that the point of view of those men with regard to what provision should be and can be made for their return to civil life, or their "change-over", should be represented by someone who knows something of the difficulties which they have had to meet. By that I mean the point of view should be represented by someone who has been in the fighting services and, more than that, someone who has been in the fighting. That is the first principle, that the point of
view of the man himself or of the body of men should be represented by those who know that point of view, either by direct experience of their own or by learning from those who have had direct experience; I mean their point of view in connection with the measures which must be considered for the purpose of helping to rehabilitate ex-service men. The list of such measures or at least of subjects dealt with in that way is really a long one.
I have an opportunity, as probably many other hon. members have had, of reading the resolutions and reports on rehabilitation in the proceedings of the Canadian Legion convention in Vancouver a very short time ago. Those resolutions, on various subjects which vitally affect ex-service men, cover page after page. I am sure I do not need to say, for hon. members of the house and the country will agree, that the Canadian Legion all down through the years has represented the exservice men in a very fine way in connection with legislation and individual measures which might be for their benefit. On the whole I think one can say that their attitude has been very tolerant, helpful and considerate. With many of the resolutions, of course, I may not agree entirely, but the tone, temper and general nature of those resolutions are such as to commend them to the public generally, I should think, and would indicate that they took a serious view of their responsibilities in helping to represent the ex-service man. But I am sure they would be the first to. agree that men in the fighting services and on the fighting fronts to-day would be glad also to have the benefit of the representations which . come from those fighting fronts, from men who are there and men who come from there, that they may help in moulding the legislation and measures which are to be for the benefit of those men when they come home.
That is the first office which the three fighting services wish to help perform. Flowing from that, as hon. members will see, is this point, that there is a real matter of military efficiency involved. That comes about in this way, that the more assured the men in the fighting services, who are on the beaches of France or in Italy to-night, and the more assured their dependents are that their interests are being and will be looked after by those who know something about the situation, and less their worry and consequently the better for military efficiency. That also is a factor which the defence services, I think quite properly, consider important in connection with this activity which they are undertaking. They consider that the morale of the fighting men, the morale of the dependents of the fighting

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
men, and the morale of the country generally, benefits from an active interest being shown and active and effective work being done to help see to it that the measures taken are worthy of the men and women themselves and of the service they are giving overseas. So that each department has set up an adviser on discharge affairs; in two departments they are called advisers, while I believe the Department of National Defence for Air calls the officer the director of demobilization.
They have not a large staff, but they are charged with the responsibility in two different aspects. First let me say this, that they are not charged with the routine of demobilization of the soldiers. By routine of demobilization I mean the sort of medical examination they shall take, where the examinations shall be held, the make-up of the boards, the matter of pay, the forms to be used on discharge or demobilization, the arrangements regarding transportation. They do not deal with these matters of routine. At the present time they would not deal with the order in which demobilization shall take place. That is to say, that for the present at least they do not advise on the formula which will be adopted to decide when men will be demobilized first when general demobilization is attained.
It is not routine that they are dealing with. That routine will involve, when the time comes, putting the branch of the adjutant-general, which has been getting men into the services, into reverse, and taking the men out of the services, by making the change-over to civilian life. That routine is not anything 'that any two or three or half a dozen men can do. It will require the activities of the whole man-power side of the adjutant-general's branch, and probably more.
What those men are dealing with is not merely routine. That is to say, it is not simply the mechanics of turning men out into civil life, through the use of certain procedure and forms. But what they are dealing with is the welfare of the men who are being discharged, the matter of the amenities which can be provided for them, and the matter of the aid which can be given to them, in order that they may be absorbed, and absorbed properly, into civil life.
I just wish to deal here with two phases of that activity. First, it will take the phase of activity within the service, activity while men are still serving. That involves, some day, the matter of vocational training. There will come a time in the war when operational activities will cease-and pray God it may come soon. I, as Minister of National Defence

have very little hope that it may come soon, but we must plan for it when it does come;
I wish the house and country to understand what we are trying to do. What we will face at some time is a period of inactivity in the army, because there cannot be general demobilization all at once. And when that period of inactivity comes we will have to arrange that those periods are utilized to give useful vocational training while men are still in the army, training which will anticipate the training which will be given later by the Department of Pensions and National Health, or by the Department of Veterans' Affairs, and which will gear into that. That is a matter for planning and advice by those officials.
They will also have to be in close touch with the educational activities of the respective defence services. That education is being carried on to-day, for the primary purpose of making the man a more efficient soldier and, secondly, to be useful in helping the man to be a better and a more productive citizen. It is in connection with this latter objective that these officials will help to plan. Then there will be measures for their assistance in connection with their discharge.
The matter of clothing allowance has been mentioned. That matter of clothing allowance is one which is looked after by the three defence services. That matter of the assessment of or the fixing of a clothing allowance and advising on it, and comparing it with those of other countries, and seeing what is fair and reasonable, is a matter which would be within their purview, I would say. The matter of leave which a man gets on discharge is another thing which would come directly within the defence departments, the army, the navy and the air force. These officers would advise on that. Then there is the matter of war service gratuity. Here again these officers will study and advise, taking account of the various representations and suggestions made, and the conditions in this country affecting such assistance.
I could go on to discuss other matters, but I do wish to say further that their job will also be to plan and advise on arrangements to inform sailors and soldiers and airmen while they are in the army, and while they are still serving, and while they are still fighting, of the provision which is being made for them when the time comes for discharge.
Those are the activities in the army. While they may, and do, refer to general demobilization, we must not forget that discharges are taking place continuously. In the last sixteen weeks, for instance, we have discharged from the army about 11,000 men. Those men being

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
discharged from day to day have to be discharged properly and have to be looked after when they are discharged from the three services. We would like to have the activity of these officers to begin early and not wait for general demobilization, in order to take in the large numbers of men who are discharged from time to time. Those are activities which are taking place within the armed services.
The other activity is one which perhaps the house may think may be apt to infringe upon the Department of Pensions and National Health or the Department of Labour. Those activities have to do with the measure which would take effect after discharge. I mean, for instance, how much we will allow a man, or how much the Department of Pensions and National Health will allow a man while he is on vocational training. Or it may be the matter of veterans' homes, or many other post-discharge benefits.
You may say that the fighting services have not anything to do with those matters. But they do have ideas, and those ideas are from the men in the armed forces themselves.
Measures of that kind, as I said a moment ago, are referred to in the resolutions passed .by the legion. They are very many in number, and the items covered a great many objectives. All those matters are things on which these officers will help to plan and advise.
I am not going to talk about the merits of these matters. I think most members will agree with me when I say that the most important and the most outstanding measure, either of benefit or right, which the government could provide for in the interests of the men and women of the services when they are discharged is the matter of full employment. And if full employment is provided, a great many problems may never arise.
In that connection, obviously, there will arise questions in connection with civil service employment. Then there will be questions of the status of ex-service men in respect of government industries which have been converted from war-time to peace-time activities. What shall the status of ex-service men be in respect of those? Then there are questions of administration in connection with the service man's right to employment in their own jobs, and so on. There will arise questions involving the Department of Reconstruction and the Department of Labour. There will arise questions in connection with the Veterans' Land Act, which has already been passed. There will arise questions of vocational training, and the allowances which will be made and the facilities which may be provided. There will be questions with regard to the men engaged in the
fisheries. The measures to deal with these subjects will be proper matters for planning and advice by these officers in the three defence services, sitting in with the officers of the Department of Pensions and National Health.
There has been a great deal of discussion about small business, and other occupations and professions, in respect of which assistance has been suggested. Then there will be the question of pensions and treatment, which is always with us. And there will be questions regarding allowances for ex-service men on training or treatment. We believe that the officers of the three services can help in planning and advising on such matters.
I wish to close by repeating that the desire of the service departments is-and it is fully understood by the Department of Pensions and National Health, and by the Department of Labour, and I am sure will be agreed to by the Department of Reconstruction-that these officers function in integration with and geared in with the activities of these other departments, not to take over or infringe on any of their functions, but to help by planning and advice, with a knowledge of the point of view of those who serve in the armed forces. You will find that most of their work will be done by way of interdepartmental committees or boards on which the officers representing the armed services will sit down with the officials of other departments and endeavour to work out common problems, bringing to all concerned the point of view of the men and women in the fighting forces.
I have taken longer than I had expected, but I just wanted to make that explanation. I have spoken particularly of army activities, but I have endeavoured to represent the point of view of my colleagues, the minister for air and the minister for naval services. We feel that in this way we may be able to furnish some assistance to the men and the women in the fighting services and their dependents who are bearing the real burden and paying the real cost of this war in separation and anxiety and sorrows, in wounds and in life itself.
