speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the house will be pleased to know that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is going to set up this new organization, representative of the three fighting services, to cooperate with this new department which is being set up. I quite agree with him that such an organization was lacking in the last war, and I agree with him also as to the possibilities of such an organization being of great assistance in this war.
There is no doubt that when the men are about to be discharged from the armed services they are in a great hurry to get home, and they do not understand all the regulations and all the provisions that have been made for their benefit until it is too late. Then they are sorry that they were not a little more cautious in the first place. This new organization which the Minister of National Defence has spoken of will be of great assistance. He mentioned that it would be its duty to look after the welfare of the men and that it would contain men of experience with army life who would be in a position to advise the men of the armed forces as to their new associations in civilian life.
The minister also referred to the matter of clothing and said that it would be part of 
the duty of this new organization to advise the new department on the amount of clothing that would be required upon discharge. I wish to say a wrord about that and I think this is about as good a time as any to say it.
I am sure that if this new organization is conversant with the needs of the soldiers when they return to civilian life it will realize that the amount, of $65 which is now allowed for clothing allowance is certainly not sufficient for the soldiers to make a change-over from active service to civilian life. I would suggest to the Minister of National Defence that this new organization would be well advised to make out a list of the essential items of clothing required by the men upon discharge in order that they may start out decently clothed in civilian life. Let this organization figure out if it requires one suit or two suits of clothes, a couple of pairs of shoes or more, an overcoat, a hat and so on, whatever they think may be required, and then, when they have the list complete, find out what it would cost at modern prices and then say: This is the amount that we recommend for a clothing allowance. I am quite sure that the minister of this new Department of Veterans* Affairs will find out that $65 will not be sufficient to provide the clothing required.
I have received I do not know how many letters on this subject. I have a file of them here. They all complain of the inadequacy of the clothing allowance. I received one such document this afternoon. It is really a petition with sixty-five names attached of men in the Canadian armed services. They are petitioning us now, pleading with members of the House of Commons to give them a greater clothing allowance than the $65 which is now provided. I do not think there can be any argument in that regard. If we were living in a country which could not provide these things it might be justifiable for us to say that we can allow only $65 for clothing, but we are certainly not living nor shall we be living after this war in a land where these things cannot very easily be produced. We have wonderful potentialities of production when we change over from war-time to peacetime production and we can produce far more than is required to satisfy all our wants. So why be niggardly about this clothing allowance? This petition which I received has names of men from Drumheller, Calgary and various other cities. The men in the armed forces are very much concerned over this clothing allowance. I hope that the Department of Veterans' Affairs will not be limited by any miserly outlook in this matter but will provide a decent clothing allowance for the men upon discharge.

Department of Veterans' Affairs
I wish to associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) in regard to giving to the returned soldier settlers clear titles to the land on which they are now settled. I am not going to go over the ground that he covered so thoroughly and ably, because he put the case in such a way that it needs no further argument. I am quite sure that the minister of pensions, the minister who will be presiding over this new Department of Veterans' Affairs, is quite conversant with the facts and is sympathetic toward the men getting clear title to their land.
In this regard I think the evidence is clear, not only in the communications which have been sent to various hon. members, including the minister himself, but in the presentations which have been made in person to the minister and his officials. I met the delegation who came here to interview the minister. The meeting with the minister was arranged by the hon. member for Battle River. The delegates were courteously received and patiently listened to; they were well pleased with their reception, and the only thing which remains is for action to be taken as a result of their interview. If no action is taken these men will be very much concerned. I am not going to argue the subject now, because I am convinced that serious consideration will be given to granting clear titles to these men. Certainly this concession should be made. It would have been much more economical if we had given the land outright at first. I am not so sure, in spite of the provisions of the new Veterans' Land Act, but that the department would be farther ahead to take a lesson from the experience we have had since the last war and give these men titles to their lands. Administration costs would be saved; departmental headaches would be avoided, and none of the difficulties which attach to the proposed operation would arise. I shall rest my argument at this point, and when the bill is under discussion in committee I may have something further to say about it.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPAKTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Before the question is put, I should like to go on record as congratulating the hon. member for Fraser Vallejo (Mr. Cruickshank) upon what he had to say to-night. I hope that chivalry and honour are sufficiently alive among us that we in this house will not allow to pass unchallenged slurs against a member who has served his country well, and served it in actual combat duty. One can only hope, also, that chivalry as'well as honour are not dead in the province of Quebec.
I suggest to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) that he call the department to be set up under this bill the department of warriors' affairs. I recommend that for two reasons. First, I have had a number of letters concerning the term "veterans" and what it meant after the last war; second, the name "warrior" is a good English word. Its definition is, "one who is experienced in war." We have in Toronto a warriors' day at the annual exhibition, and the use of the term "warrior" has always been considered favourably. It does not denote age in the way that "veteran" does.
In this connection we have to deal with a very different problem at the end of this war from that which faced us at the end of the last war. The problem is different psychologically; we are dealing with a different kind of man. It is not that he is any braver or more patriotic than the soldier of the last war, but he has had a great deal more technical training. In the last war the fundamentals of service were that you should be able to march, that you should be able to shoot, that you should be able to keep yourself clean and that you should keep your head down. There was really only one weapon that you had to understand and that was the rifle; later on, the Lewis machine gun. An hon. member adds "trench mortar", but trench mortars were a specialist weapon, and it was not until quite late in the last war that they became plentiful. But in this war the infantryman has to know at least seven weapons; he has to be pretty well informed about tactics, and he has to be able to carry on and think for himself as an individual. No more is it true-and this is, I think, one fundamental difference between this war and the last-that a sergeant-major may get up and say, "You are not supposed to think", as sergeant-majors used to do in the last war. In this war you are supposed to think, and you are given a great deal of intensive training.
When the men who served in the present war are discharged they will be trained men; they will have been trained to use a number of weapons and to think for themselves, and this will be a great asset, because many opportunities will arise in Canada in the shape of new industries. The radio industry, the science of electronics, the plastic industries, the aircraft industry are examples; all these will require many men, but the men they will require will be those who will be trained in the new sciences. Those sciences are not taught at the technical schools or the universities; they are taught only in the plants which are established
390S
Department of Veterans' Affairs

to produce these new materials-some of them still on the secret list. They offer to our men a great future, and I suggest to the minister that he make a survey of these industries and arrange with them to take for training men discharged from the army.
There has been a great deal of talk about education; but after a man has been in the army, the air force or the navy for four or five years, he is not psychologically prepared to go back to school or university. He wants to start out at once to earn a living. This point of view is, I think, well expressed in a letter I received from an airman serving in the far east. I will quote one paragraph because it seems to me significant. He says:
I don't think that the average man, in the service which, I know, wishes or expects any sort of a handout after this war is won. Yet I believe that, for our own and the dominion's protection, some method of placement should be adopted just so long as no compulsory placement is attempted. A great "to do" is being raised about the educational opportunities the government will provide. Very good for a few but hardly a plan which will affect the many. For example, of the forty or so Canadians with whom I am in touch (all rather above average in educational standards) only two are seriously able to consider future education at the government's expense-and it is doubtful if even one of those will take advantage of the offers.
That is an individual case, but I consider it symptomatic of the position of the majority of the members of our armed forces to-day. I do not think there will be a strong desire on the part of many to go back to school or to go back to the university. Let us look at the position in which these men will find themselves. First of all, despite what critics may say, they will have had the priceless opportunity of knowing armed combat. Furthermore, they will be four or five years older. If they go back to the university they will find themselves men in classes along with mere boys. That is one o'f the psychological problems which we cannot overemphasize.
The next and very important question is the economic one. Many of these men have married; a great many of them are considering marriage, and they are four or five years older. At that age it becomes necessary for them to consider, not education but the immediate earning of a living. Therefore I believe that the first problem, as the minister has intimated, will be to provide employment in industry where expansion is most likely to take place. I make this suggestion because I understand it has been carried out elsewhere, as I shall mention in a minute.
Let me say a word with regard to the development of the farm. If there was criticism to be levelled against the administration

after the last war it was because they put men on the farm who did not know the problems of farming. Not only did they not know the problems of farming, they were psychologically not attuned to life on the farm, particularly after life in the armed services. I know of several cases where they found the loneliness of life on the farm a very serious drawback. They found the changeover from being looked after for twenty-four hours a day to being completely on their own too great a psychological change to be undergone. Many of them became unhappy because of that change.
I suggest to the minister that before he puts men on the farm he give them an opportunity to know rural work. I speak for southern Ontario, the part of Canada I know best. We have there a serious problem of soil erosion, the destruction of our forests, the depletion of our agricultural resources, caused by a lack of water through the drying up of our streams. Only an infinitesimal part of the job has been done in tackling the problem. Of the many hundreds of thousands of acres in this rich agricultural belt, only King township and the interlobate moraine of the Ganaraska valley have been adequately surveyed.
I suggest that immediate steps be taken to create survey parties to make a complete study of the reconstruction and rehabilitation or the bringing back of this great agricultural belt of southern Ontario to the state in which it was before we and our ancestors did it such grievous damage by cutting trees, destroying streams and so on. No one who knows that part of the country can underestimate the seriousness of the situation. Let me give one example. In the Peel plain, the great fertile belt represented by the leader of the opposition, seventy per cent of the water in the streams has been lost from the early days. That is a serious situation we must face.
I suggest that one of the first things that men who want to go on farms after the war should be asked to do is to make up survey parties to study the conditions of the land. This would do a number of things. First of all, it wouid provide an essential service.
I stress that because it is essential. We have to understand, we have to have much more knowledge of the problems of the land than we have at the present time. Second, it would give these men coming out of the army an opportunity to know what rural life was like, what farm life was like and what the problems of farming were. They would be given that opportunity at first hand immediately on coming out of the army. They would

Department of Veterans' Affairs
not have to take the irrevocable step of deciding to go on the farm before they realized what rural life was like. I think this is very important, particularly when we consider the type of man being discharged to-day from the army, navy and air force and the type of man who will be discharged at the end of the war.
Another suggestion I should like to offer is that if this country is to fulfil its destiny, that destiny is closely associated with the development of our minerals. I shall not go into the state of our mineral resources to-day, but let me say just one thing. Of our present splendid production eighty-four per cent comes from mines discovered over twenty-five years ago and only five per cent from mines discovered since 1930. That is an extremely dangerous, even perilous, situation not appreciated, I am afraid, by this government or its predecessor.
One of the immediate problems of the postwar period will be the discovery and development of our mineral resources which now are merely indicated. I again suggest to the minister that he, in conjunction with the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) undertake now the establishment of numerous survey parties. Subcommittee No. 2 which has to do with reconstruction said that thousands of prospectors would be needed. Professor Wallace used the word "thousands". That number will be needed if we are to take any recognition of what Russia, a country less blest with mineral resources than ours, is doing. Immediately before the war they had something like three hundred thousand men actively engaged in exploration for minerals. I suggest that here is an immediate opportunity for men being discharged from the army. It does two things. It gives them a waiting period in which they are actively employed doing useful and essential work. It gives them an opportunity to know the mineral industry; whether they want to go in for it or not, it gives many men who may be psychologically not adjusted to civil life an opportunity to work for a year or two to adjust themselves to the slower tempo of civilian life in Canada.
This is very important, because in our age of mass production many men will be asked to do factory jobs which are repetitive. Any hon. members who know the large automotive industry will know what working on an assembly line means. I ask them to put themselves in the position of a young airman, who comes out of combat after having flown a Lancaster bomber with five thousand horsepower at his finger-tips, with bomb bays filled with weapons capable of producing acres of
destruction, who is asked to go to a factory and told that his job is to do one of these routine jobs for eight hours a day. I do not think he is going to like it. I do not think it is fair to ask him to do it. That will be one of our problems. There is one thing more. Before the war many men were engaged as salesmen. They were selling mundane things, such as breakfast foods, soap and other household articles. Put yourself in the position of a young man from Normandy who is told that his job is to sell goods to this grocery store and that grocery store. I do not think he is psychologically prepared on discharge to do so. Some recognition must be taken of that fact.
I have seen a scheme in California which I believe is working quite satisfactorily to a degree. The major industries of California have set up a board. They have a central office in the larger towns. I think they have one in Los Angeles and one in San Francisco. I am sure of San Francisco, but I am not sure of Los Angeles. Every manufacturer, every industrialist and some of the larger growers send to this central board their requirements for labour and those they can employ. They tell the type of man they want and the type of work to be done. There is an opportunity for men awaiting discharge to go to this clearing house and be interviewed by this organization. A man who has been a mechanic may be offered certain work. A man is asked what he wants to do, whether he wants to go back to the university, and so on. The manufacturers cooperate in putting him at the type of work for which he thinks he is best suited.
I know the minister will say that we have selective service, but at the present time our selective service is interested in one thing and one thing only, namely, getting men. I know of an incident that took place in Vancouver the other day. A young man who was an engineer wanted to do a special type of work for which he was fitted. He went to selective service and they told him that men were wanted in the shipyards. They said to him: "The only thing we can suggest to you is that you go to the shipyards." They did that because men were needed in the shipyard at that time. Probably they still need them there. This is not a criticism of national selective service. That is their function, and that is what they are doing. In my opinion this other system is working out extremely well in California. They do something else. They visit the hospitals. Every manufacturer with a plant, growers and all other people interested, keep a list of the men who are wanted. The board says, "here is a man who

Department of Veterans' Affairs

has lost his leg", or, "here is a man. who has had a serious back injury". Each individual searches his operation and says, "I can use a man with one leg in such and such a way; I can use a man with a back injury." The man in the hospital is interviewed, and in many cases he is guaranteed employment even while he is undergoing treatment there. That has a tremendous psychological effect on the well-being of that individual and it is an important factor in his cure.
These comments are by way of suggestion. The problem of the reemployment of our men is probably the major difficulty we shall have to face after the defeat of the axis powers, and in that connection I think two things should be kept in mind. First, we should remember that warfare is the science of destruction; that men are trained-magnificently trained-to destroy the enemy instantly, whereas in peace time the opposite factor is paramount. In warfare it is a question of kill or be killed; the cost is unimportant. In peace time it is a matter of conservation, and the cost is very important. That will be a definite problem in the changeover. The next point, and with this I close, is that these men do not want gratitude. They want to feel that they are doing something useful for this country for which they have fought, and it is important that the work they are asked to do shall be essential to the future of Canada, just as essential as the magnificent work they are doing to-day on the beachhead in Normandy.

Instead we find such words as these: in section 5, "any person"; in section 6, "persons"; in section 7, "persons who served with the naval, military or air forces of His Majesty", and in section 7(b), "such other persons as may be deemed advisable," and so on. Last evening the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) said that he did not think it would work out to have the reestablishment of veterans and civilians put under the new Department of Veterans' Affairs, and the minister replied, "That is not the intention." If that is not the intention then I ask why such powers1 should be included in this bill. I am not an expert on the drafting of statutes, but I believe that this bill as drafted is open to a great deal of criticism; in fact it is my feeling that it should be redrafted; that the powers of the

minister should be more clearly defined; that they should be limited to veterans; that the word "veterans" should be defined in a clear and broad way, and that these other extensive powers which are given to the minister should be cut out of the bill.
In that connection there is one other matter I should like to mention. Section 7(d) provides for the marking or stamping of artificial limbs or appliances. I should like to ask the minister why both those expressions should be used. I have looked in the dictionary and I find that the word "appliances" means, "a thing applied as a means to an end."

In the forceful, eloquent and sane speech made by the honourable and gallant member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) during the course of this debate he asked a question which I though very pertinent and which I believe must be answered. This was the question: "Are we to treat our men as well when they return to be trained for peace as we did when they were trained for war in our hour of need?" That question cannot be lightly brushed aside; it deserves and must be given an answer. It has been pointed out already, but I am going to refer to it again, that when a man enlists he is paid SI .30 a day in cash, or about $39 a month. If he has to live out he receives, in addition, $36.50 a month. His wife receives a dependents' allowance of $39.12, with additional allowances for children. This makes a total family income of $115.62 a month, plus allowances for children. But when a man comes out of the army or, to use 'the words of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) this evening, when a man changes over, which is perhaps a better term, and takes up vocational training for the purpose of improving his , position in civilian life, under the regulations he receives $60 a month, while his wife receives $20, with similar allowances for children. In other words, when he begins to train in the army he receives a total of $115.62 a month, but when he begins to train for civilian life he and his family receive only

Department of Veterans' Affairs
$80 a month, a reduction of about thirty per cent. Personally I do not believe this is good enough. I do not believe it is too much to ask that returned men who want to qualify themselves for positions in civil life should receive the same rate of pay as they received when they first entered the army. We must be just before we are generous; we must pay our debts before we make gifts, and I say that we owe to these returned men a debt which we should pay in full before we vote $76,000,000 a year or some similar amount to that institution we call UNRRA. Our duty to our returned men is one of our first responsibilities. This evening the Minister of National Defence said that certain directors or advisers were to be appointed, and when that is done I hope these gentlemen will give this matter some consideration.

Now that they are appointed I hope they will give this matter some consideration with a view to bringing the allowances awarded to returned men during the time they are taking vocational training up to the amount they received 'when they entered the army.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer. I wish to support what has been said by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) and a number of other members when they asked that veterans of the last war who took up farms under the soldier settlement scheme be given a clear title, although they have not paid for their farms in full.
I believe that a man should live up to his agreements and should meet his obligations. But there are some cases when this is quite impossible, and I think the situation in which these men in the prairie provinces find themselves is one of those cases. I met a delegation that came to Ottawa not long ago from the prairie provinces to speak on behalf of those soldier settlers who have been unable to pay in full for their farms. I must confess that I was not greatly impressed by a considerable part of their brief, but I was impressed by the men themselves. One could not look at them and talk with them without being impressed. One could not look them over without realizing that for many years past they had had a tremendously difficult task, that they had fought against very hard odds, and that they had done the best they could under the circumstances. It was clear, however, that fate was against them. Someone has said that the cards were stacked against them.

I think these men might be given a clear title to those farms on the ground that a mutual mistake was made. The mistake was this, that the soldier settlement board overvalued those farms. Then the veterans who went on the farms made a mistake in that they thought the farms would produce a great deal more revenue than they did. That mistake, in both cases, was owing to the fact that the farms had been purchased and arrangements made in boom times. I would urge the minister and the government to give this matter their most serious consideration. After talking to those men I felt that we could not afford to let them go off the land, and that we would be making a great mistake if we let men of their character leave their farms.
The figures show that from September t, 1939, to December 31, 1943, 2,418 of these settlers left their farms, or an average of 606 a year in the last four and a half years. If we let men of that kind get off the land we are making a great mistake. They are men who volunteered to do their duty at the commencement of the last war. They went overseas and their sons are overseas to-day. Their sons, and their daughters, too, are. in the>
[DOT]services, and they look forward to coming home. If their homes are disappearing at. the rate of 606 a year a great many of them will have no homes to return to when the war is over.
As I said before, I think people should meet their obligations and live up to their agreements, even if those agreements are hard ones. But this is a case in which I believe that an exception should be made, not only in the interests of the men and their families, but in the interest of the country at large. I would urge as strongly as I can that the. request of the men to have clear title be granted. I realize that there are difficulties in the way, but I think they could be overcome and they should not prevent the government from, granting this request and giving those men clear titles to their land.

speechtext:
I regard that as important. I was particularly interested in the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) where he talked about an integrating service that would look after a man even before he left the service and give him, as it were, a start so that he could make better progress under the care of the new department. I think this is very important to the navy because it seems to me that outside the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve officers, or the men who are real sailors, and who learned their vocation on the sea, the place of navy men in the merchant marine after the war is open to question.
There must be many men in the navy who will want to follow the sea after the war. Canada was not always sea-conscious. But with so many men from all parts of Canada joining the navy, and with the enthusiasm that exists throughout Canada to-day in connection with the navy, also in view of the fact that with the building of the St. Lawrence waterways Canada will be a sea-going country as far as the head of the lakes, there will be a greater opportunity for many men to continue their vocations on the sea.
I am not speaking with full knowledge at the moment, but it appears to me that in Canada especially a naval officer will have little standing in the merchant marine after the war. He will not have a certificate. He may not even have the service that is required. In my view, some provision should be made whereby men who are now naval officers will be able to fit themselves to be officers in the merchant marine. And, with regard to ratings in the navy, it seems to me that any boy who wishes to follow the sea in Canada should be given that chance to fit himself to advance in the service during peace time. He should be able to advance in what is now known as the merchant navy. The education is different. A naval officer in the navy is taught to destroy, and his education is that of destruction and of defeating the enemy. On the other hand, the man in the merchant marine is taught differently; he must preserve property and overcome the elements, and he must know certain principles of business in order that he may operate profitably and successfully. So that there is here a great chance for coordination. Also there is a great chance to find employment. This will be the right kind of employment for men who were sea-going in the navy during the war.
Then, with regard to merchant sailors, it is true that for the first time in our history the government by order in council has legislation which enables a man in the merchant marine to get a pension or to be compensated if he is hurt in connection with direct or indirect

action against the enemy. However, after discharge there is not much provision for a member of the merchant marine, and some consideration should be given to the care of those men who are in the merchant marine and who, after discharge, will have a claim for service rendered.
I have heard considerable complaints from men and officers of the R.C.N.R. that they were at a disadvantage in being in the navy during the war; being in a minority. A naval reserve man does not feel at home behind a desk. He is perhaps not so well qualified to work in an executive position on shore, but he is a real man upon the sea. At the start of the war they were the men you had to depend on to carry on the sea work until such time as other men could be trained to go on board ships, and their direction and knowledge was invaluable. Hon. members will see that the merchant marine and the navy are almost one in their interests. Their future is entwined, and I trust that this department will regard the men of the merchant marine as worthy of its consideration. In that way we shall be not only helping the men of the service but helping the marine and helping to build up the country in the future; because, Mr. Speaker, no country was ever great that did not have a big marine trade. Canada is eminently suited to developing a big marine trade if our people will only make the effort. On the east, west and north we have the ocean, besides the great lakes and waterways, and we can develop a great marine. So that I hope that these men who are serving in the merchant marine, with little glory and no glamour, will get the consideration they deserve. That to me .is an added reason why I would enthusiastically support the bill which is now before the house for the creation of this new department,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a word before the second reading passes. I think this debate has provided a very good example of the heights to which parliament can rise on certain occasions in discussing vital subjects in a war-lime period. While considerable time has been taken up in discussing the problem which is now immediately confronting parliament, the creation of a ministry of veterans' affairs, I cannot conceive how in a period such as this parliament could spend its time to better advantage than in hearing the comments, views and constructive criticism of the men and women present representing the 245 constituencies of Canada, speaking on behalf of the men who are giving so much by way of service and sacrifice that we may continue as a free

Department of Veterans' Affairs
parliament in this land. I think it has been time well spent. I think we can take some pride in the manner in which this parliament has risen, to its task. The unity of purpose and of thought and of opinion which has characterized this debate may appropriately provide an example for our discussion of many other subjects which parliament in war time might tackle and attempt to solve.
I believe that most of us recognize our responsibilities to the men and the women who will come back. Primarily, of course, this is the government's responsibility. But I want to go a little farther than that and say that coincidental with the responsibilities and the duty of the government, parliament has an obligation to the men and the women who come back. There is, too, a definite responsibility resting upon the individual civilian toward these men and women who, upon discharge, will be rehabilitating themselves into normal civilian life. The meshing of these men and women into the social and economic life of our country is not going to be an easy task, but it will be made a little easier for them, a little easier for the government and a little easier for the whole officialdom which will be handling these delicate problems of great magnitude if all the citizens of Canada will do their part, as it is their bounden duty to do. Our citizens on the home front have suffered inconvenience, of course, in a certain fashion through these war years, but their sufferings have been small in comparison with the services and the sacrifices which have been made by the men and the women whom we must rehabilitate upon their return. This is one way in which the civilian population of Canada can make a further contribution to those who have already contributed so very much more than we have who have not been privileged to serve. So that I say to you, Mr. Speaker, to-night that nothing less than the best for those who served will be good enough for this government and this parliament and for the Canadian .people to give to rehabilitate these men and women when they return.
I rose to-night largely to pay a tribute to a group of citizens in Canada who are shouldering in a masterly way the responsibilities which devolve partly at least on our citizen community. The Department of Pensions and National Health has set up, as you know Mr. Speaker, rehabilitation committees across Canada. I have already had the privilege of having had something to do with these committees. A week from tonight I am leaving Ottawa to go nearly three hundred miles to attend a meeting of the
rehabilitation committee in the south end of my own constituency, after having refused a good many of what I thought were much less important obligations, because I thought this was something we owe to our men and women who are serving, no matter whether we are members of parliament or private citizens. If we cannot do that much to help those who have been doing so much for us, the problem of rehabilitation becomes more serious, more critical and more dangerous perhaps than we had at first considered it.
I am glad to-night to pay my tribute to these men who are serving on these rehabilitation committees across Canada in a voluntary capacity. They are coming to grips with the present day problems, because they are closely in touch with local conditions and are concerning themselves with admitting these men and women of the armed forces into our civilian life again in a way which is probably more practical than some of the suggestions which have been made in the course of this debate. I am hopeful that by virtue of the work of these committees the first step will have been taken toward a revived consciousness on the part of our citizens generally of their obligations to those who return from this war. With that I might leave the work of these rehabilitation committees, on which I am hopeful that so many of our citizens will find an opportunity to serve and take part in solving the problems that lie ahead. I hope that the work will be continued. I trust that it will include the problems of veterans generally. I do not like the word "veteran" very well; I trust the minister may be able to find some better terminology.

I refrained from entering into the debate on the second reading of the bill, for the specific reason just mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. To my mind the principle of the bill was so simple that it did not involve at all the comprehensive discussion on pensions and treatment and hospitalization and rehabilitation which we have had for the last three days. It was purely a change of the method of administration from the old-established method to the contemplated method. However, I agree with the hon. member and definitely with the leader of the opposition that the time has not been wasted, that it has not been spent in vain, because this house has lived up to its old tradition of a splendid unity of thought, and, I trust, a unity' of action, in regard to the problems of our returning ex-service men. I think the history of legislation in this house for the last twenty-five years is not and has not been the effort of any one party; it has been the result of the conjoint sympathies and work and efforts of every single party in the dominion. That is the spirit of the debate which has just been concluded. I wish to thank hon. members in all parts of the house for their sympathetic attitude toward the department over which I temporarily preside, and the kindly references made from many sources to the humble minister of that department.
There was one reference, however, which was made that I must take exception to: it was in regard to there being "too many brass hats" in the Department of Pensions and National Health. In the rehabilitation work of our department, the associate deputy minister served in the ranks. The superintendent of vocational training served in the ranks, winning the military medal and bar, and subsequently obtained his commission in the field.	The superintendent of educational
training served in the ranks. The deputy minister, being a medical officer at the time of his enlistment, naturally held commissioned rank.	The assistant deputy minister also
served in the ranks. In fact all other senior officers, some twenty of whom enlisted in the ranks, held rank not above that of major, with the exception of the present chairman of

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
the Canadian pension commission, whose present rank was obtained during service overseas in the present war which followed outstanding service in a junior capacity in the great war. The chief of the orthopaedic and surgical appliances division, that branch which has the most intimate contact with those casualties which require and deserve the most sympathetic and active attention, the amputation cases, was a sapper in the last war during which he suffered amputation of both legs and the loss of one eye. Of the nine pension commissioners, six served in the ranks. While the reference to brass hats may be proper in some direction, it is not justified by the facts with reference to the staff of this department. Practically eighty or ninety per cent of these men went through the ranks during the last war.
I had intended to make a certain analysis of the various aspects of the problems with which the Department is concerned, but on reflection I think our duty at this time is to examine the particular sections of the bill when we reach them, and to discuss questions of policy affecting' pensions, the effect of treatment, the effect of hospitalization and the effect of rehabilitation when the civil estimates of the Department of Pensions and National Health are up for consideration.
I think it was. the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) who yesterday gave a brief resume of the history of this department, commencing with the old Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment in 1918 and coming down to 1928 when the Department of Pensions and National Health Act was passed. My hon. friend suggested that the privileges granted under the sections of this bill are possibly based upon the soldiers of the old war. Possibly there is some element of truth in that, but I say that it is vital to protect the privileges of those who served in the great war as well as to do what we are doing under this measure, to establish new opportunities and to grant new privileges to those serving in the present war.

compensate for any handicap, physical or otherwise, arising out of military service. Second, to give the member of the forces a fair start in civil life. Third, to have permanently available those services which the country can and should render to its war veterans throughout their lives.
Perhaps I could give my hon. friends the latest figures with regard to pensions as it may be of interest. On April 30 of this year the grand total of pension awards made by the commission for all classes of pensions arising out of service in the present war was 13,215, and the total annual liability amounted to $6,795,593. With respect to members of the armed forces, 7,591 awards were for disabilities and 5,158 were for dependents of those who have given their lives. There were twenty-six disability pensions awarded to women members of the forces.
The commission have awarded 410 pensions with respect to death or disability sustained by members of the merchant marine, fishermen, members of the auxiliary services, civilian government employees, R.C.M.P. special constable guards, members of civilian defence forces and members of the corps of firefighters for service in the United Kingdom. The number of awards of pensions under section 11, subsection 3 of the Pension Act is 1,028, including 611 awards for disability and 417 for death. Up to December 31, 1943, Canada had augmented to the Canadian scale 1,192 pensions awarded by the British government to Canadians serving in the imperial forces.
I should like also to deal, but not at the present time, with the question of hospitalization because it has been raised in this debate and I feel that at some time I should give a complete answer to the questions raised.
I come now specifically to the points raised last night by the hon. member for Vancouver South who dealt with certain sections of the bill. As I said before, it was considered whether there should be two parts, one dealing with great war veterans and the other dealing with veterans of the present war, or one bill embracing all veterans. The present . bill covers all veterans. It was necessary to retain all language relating to former rights and privileges lest some right or privilege of the former veterans be sacrificed. These have been extended to the present war veterans, so that they would have the same rights, but provisions have been added to ensure ample extension to meet future requirements.
My hon. friend suggested that re-housing should be included in the measure. In the opinion of those who have been advising me-
Department of Veterans' Affairs

and this measure has been very carefully reviewed, not only by our own officials but by the officials of the Department of Justice-the phrase "reestablishment in civil life" is broad enough to cover practically all the suggestions made last night. If special legislation is decided upon, the bill provides that the functions of the minister shall extend and apply as well to all such other matters as may be designated or assigned to the minister by the governor in council.
Then my hon. friend referred to the repatriation of dependents. Extensive and successful repatriation of soldiers and their dependents was efficiently carried out after the last war by the cooperation of three departments. First, there was the Department of Immigration which controls the admission into Canada of all persons. Second, there was the Department of Militia and Defence which still actively controlled the serving soldier whose dependents were accompanying him. Third, there was the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment which was directly concerned with the establishment in civil life of the soldier and his dependents after discharge.
Then my lion.- friend referred to the payment of gratuities. This is and must remain the responsibility of the services since they alone have the service records upon which the gratuities are calculated, and the actual administration will be carried on either by the Department of National Defence or that department along with the Department of Finance.

I had intended to speak on pensions and other matters to-night but will accept the suggestion of the minister to take them up when the civil estimates are before the committee; but I wish to say a few words on the Veterans' Land Act.
In connection with the Veterans' Land Act I was very glad to see the increase in the amount granted as credit for land. It has been extended from $3,600 to $4,800. I am now going to make a suggestion to the minister that the amount for implements and equipment be also increased. At the present time it stands at $1,200. When one considers the present prices that the settlers will have to pay I feel that is not nearly sufficient. I hope the government will give that matter their earnest attention.
The next point I should like to touch on is that of interest. I believe that could be reduced a little more as well. There is no necessity for the settlers to pay three and a half per cent interest as suggested. Another lesson we learned with regard to the treatment of the soldiers under the old settlement board act is the price at which they were compelled to sell their products. It does not make any difference if the land and equipment are given as a gift if the settlers are compelled to sell their products at as low prices as were the settlers under the old Soldier Settlement Board 'Act, they are bound to go broke. I am going to suggest to the government that any year the prices at which farmers sell their product are lower than the prices obtaining to-day, the government should give the settlers credit for the difference between present prices and those at which they are compelled to sell. As the committee is well aware, the department only operates institutions in a few of the larger centres in Canada and, as a consequence, it has been necessary, and I may say highly desirable, that patients be cared for in municipal, religious and other institutions throughout the country, which practice has been followed since and during the great war.
During the fiscal year just ended some
2.431.000	patient days treatment were furnished by the department. Of these over
908.000	were furnished in non-departmental institutions.
The general custom has been that the department should enter into a contract with these larger non-departmental hospitals whereby the hospitals undertook to give service to patients and the department undertook to compensate the hospital at an agreed rate per patient per day. Although, as stated, many such formal contracts have been entered into,

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
there are many hundreds of hospitals throughout Canada, and those used outside of Canada, with which no such formal contract has been made by reason of their location, size or the limited extent to which patients may be admitted as the occasion demands.
When the drafting officers appreciated that there was no specific authority in the statute authorizing the minister to make such arrangement, they considered that the present bill would be strengthened by the inclusion of a definite clause conferring this power. Clause 6 as it appears in the bill was the result.
When, however, the administrative officers of the department had had an opportunity of considering the implications of clause 6 as it appears in bill No. 83, they found it might impose a great hardship upon numbers of individual ex-service men, apart altogether from the increased administrative complications.
Let us consider the case of a veteran living in a remote part of the country where the department has no hospital but where there is a small municipal or other institution which serves the requirements of the area.
In the event of this man becoming suddenly ill from a condition with respect to which he is entitled to treatment from the department, our desire would be to arrange for his admission to the nearest hospital and to have medical services provided by the nearest qualified practitioner.
Such an arrangement involves an undertaking to pay and is in effect a contract between the department on the one hand and the hospital and the doctor on the other hand. It has been customary to make such agreement by telegram or telephone in emergency cases for many years. In fact, under the present regulations, the department may accept responsibility for a limited period preceding the reporting of the case to the department if the serious illness of the patient was the reason for his not making application.
Clause 6 as now before this committee would, if adopted, preclude the department from making these informal arrangements for treatment in such emergent or far-removed cases until the department had entered into a contract with the hospital and the doctor and until such contract had been ratified by order in council.
This effect was not anticipated by the legal officers who drafted the clause nor, I am sure, is it the desire of parliament and of the people of Canada that there should be any such cumbersome procedure prohibiting the prompt extension to the ex-service man of necessary medical or hospital care.	.
I illustrate the point with an extreme condition which, however, arises with a fair degree of frequency. This clause would hamper-administration in many other ways.
For example, when an ex-service man requires dental care, it is the department's practice as an economy measure to arrange,, where feasible, for his treatment by a dentist in his own locality rather than put the country to the expense of bringing the patient to a centre where the department has a salaried dental officer and of incurring further expense to reimburse him for loss of time from work which otherwise could be avoided.
The present clause 6, if adopted, would require the department to enter into contracts with every dentist in Canada or would prevent us from continuing the present economical procedure which is regularized through the medium of regulations which permit the department to establish schedule of fees for services performed by non-salaried dental an! medical officers.
